t.sandwich@41.8,-70.5:
Sandwich is the oldest town on Cape Cod, founded in 1637 by settlers from the Plymouth Colony, and it has the air of a place that has been looking at the same view for a very long time. Houses with weathered grey shingles stand around a village green, a mill pond and a small, historic grist mill, and the old Dexter Grist Mill still grinds corn on certain days. The town was home to the Boston and Sandwich Glass Company, founded in the 1820s, whose colourful pressed glass was once sold across America, and a museum on the main street displays the best pieces.

The Cape Cod Canal, completed in 1914, cuts across the base of the peninsula just beyond the town, with the Sagamore and Bourne bridges arching over it. A path runs along both banks, and watching the ships go through is a good way to spend an hour. The canal turned the Cape into an island, in the technical sense, and saved ships the long and dangerous passage around the outer shore.

The road that gives the ride its name is Route 6A, the Old King's Highway, which runs along the north shore of the Cape from Sandwich to Orleans. It is one of the loveliest roads in New England, a narrow, tree-lined lane that passes ancient houses, salt marshes, antique shops and sea captains' mansions. The speed limit is low, the bends are gentle and the surface is generally good, though the road is crowded in summer, when traffic crawls and parking is scarce. Early spring and late autumn are the quiet seasons, with fog, wind and light that is soft and silver. The Sandy Neck, a long barrier beach to the east, is a haven for birds, including piping plovers, which nest in the dunes in spring.

Sandwich has about three thousand people, with Sagamore and East Sandwich close by, and there are fuel stations and shops on Route 6A and on the main roads. For a wider choice, the nearest bigger town is Mashpee, about twelve kilometres south. Traffic on the bridges over the canal can back up badly on summer weekends, so aim to cross before eight or after six. In the off season, many restaurants and shops shut, so check before you set out.
t.essex@41.4,-72.4:
Essex is the kind of Connecticut river town that makes visitors suspect it has been arranged for their benefit. It sits on the west bank of the Connecticut River, a few kilometres from Long Island Sound, and its main street runs down to a waterfront crowded with sailboats, cruisers and old brick warehouses. It was a shipbuilding village from the seventeen hundreds, and the Oliver Cromwell, a frigate of the Continental Navy, was launched here in 1776. The Griswold Inn, which opened the same year, still serves meals in a tavern full of ship paintings and old guns, and it is possibly the oldest continuously operating inn in the country.

The river is the reason for the ride. The Connecticut is the longest in New England, and in its lower reaches it is broad, slow and tidal, with wooded hills on both sides and marshes full of ospreys and herons. Down here it flows through a landscape that is almost unspoiled, protected by decades of conservation. A steam train and riverboat run from Essex, the train going up the valley to Chester and the boat carrying passengers to the old opera house at Haddam, and the whole combination looks like a nineteenth century print.

Upstream, at Hadlyme, the road climbs to Gillette Castle, a fantastic medieval fortress of fieldstone built between 1914 and 1919 by the actor William Gillette, who made his fortune playing Sherlock Holmes on stage. He designed it himself, down to the wooden door locks, and he left it to the state on his death. The views over the river are superb. To reach it you can ride the Chester to Hadlyme ferry, one of the oldest in America, which has crossed the river since the 1760s, a short ride on an open deck that holds just a handful of vehicles.

The roads here are narrow, wooded and winding, with tight bends, low stone walls and trees that overhang the lane. They are slow, but they reward patience, particularly in autumn. Essex has fuel nearby, but the larger town of Old Saybrook, about seven kilometres south, has the stations and supermarkets, and Deep River has more modest services. In summer the villages are crowded with visitors, and a weekday morning is the best time. Late October, with the maples red and the river steaming in the cold, is the moment to come.
t.middletown@41.4,-74.4:
Onions are the quiet fame of Orange County, New York, and the fields lie just north of Middletown. The black dirt region, a flat basin of ancient lakebed soil dark as coffee grounds, was drained in the nineteenth century and turned into some of the richest farmland in the Northeast, growing onions, lettuce, corn and sweet potatoes, and in autumn the roads are lined with trucks loaded with sacks. Middletown itself, a small city of about twenty-eight thousand, grew up as a railway junction and a manufacturing town, and its old brick downtown has a faded but friendly feel.

The ride has two halves, and this town is where they start and end. Heading west, you come quickly to the Delaware River and the road known as Hawk's Nest, a stretch of Route 97 blasted into the cliff face in the 1930s above the river between Port Jervis and Sparrowbush. It is one of the great short rides in the region, with a cliff on one side and a long drop to the river on the other, the road curling around outcrops with sharp, tight bends and a low stone wall that does not inspire confidence. Photographers and cyclists share it, so on a sunny weekend it can be busy. The view down the river, with the Pennsylvania hills opposite, is superb, and the colour in October is remarkable.

Then comes the Delaware Water Gap, where the river cuts through the Kittatinny Ridge in a deep notch, and the national recreation area covers the valley on both sides. Eagles winter along the river, and in summer canoeists drift past on the slow current. Back at Middletown, there are the Shawangunks to the north and the Hudson Highlands to the east, with their own good roads.

Fuel and services are no problem here. Middletown has stations, supermarkets, diners and hotels, and the main road carries plenty of traffic. Unlike across the river in New Jersey, where an attendant does the pumping, in New York State you fill your own tank. Mechanics are easy to find, and the town is a convenient place to start or finish the day. Goshen, a few miles away, is known for its harness racing track, one of the oldest in the country.

Take it easy on Hawk's Nest. Gravel, wet leaves and sun-glare can all catch the unwary, and the river is a long way down.
t.smugglers notch@44.6,-72.8:
Smugglers Notch is the sort of road that makes a motorcyclist grin and a camper-van driver clench. Vermont Route 108 climbs through a narrow gap between Mount Mansfield, the highest peak in the state, and Spruce Peak, and at the top, at about 660 metres, it squeezes between enormous boulders that have tumbled off the cliffs and been left where they landed. The tarmac is tight, with hairpins and blind corners, no shoulder to speak of, and in some places barely a car and a half wide. Large vehicles and trailers are banned, which is the highway department's way of admitting that physics is going to win.

The name tells the story. When the United States passed the Embargo Act in 1807, cutting off trade with Britain, Vermont farmers and merchants suddenly found their best market closed, and cattle and goods went north over the border through any pass that would take them. Later the notch was said to have served runaway slaves heading to Canada and, in Prohibition, liquor smugglers coming south. There is a long tradition of people moving things quietly through this gap, and the caves and ledges among the boulders are exactly the kind of place where one could do it. Some of the rocks have names, with one resembling an elephant's head and another a hearse.

The riding is best on a dry morning, before the day-trippers arrive. Coming from Stowe, you wind up through the forest, past the ski resort buildings, and the road narrows until the trees give way to rock walls on either side. The climb is short but intense, the descent on the Jeffersonville side opens out into farmland and long views, and the whole thing takes twenty minutes if you ride it carefully. Take it slowly, watch for gravel on the corners and for cyclists and hikers on the road, and be aware that the pass is closed to traffic in winter, usually from late autumn until well into spring.

Stowe has fuel, food and a long-established tradition of hospitality, and Morristown, with its larger population, is the nearest bigger town, about thirteen kilometres away. Johnson, on the western side, is smaller but has the basics. In early October the maples on the slopes turn red and gold, and the notch becomes a destination for leaf-peepers, so go midweek if you can. The air at the top smells of cold stone and spruce, and even on a hot day it is cool enough to be glad of a jacket.
t.roscoe trout town@41.9,-74.9:
Roscoe calls itself Trout Town USA, and it has the credentials to back the claim. The village sits in the western Catskills at the meeting of two famous fly-fishing streams, the Beaverkill and the Willowemoc, which join a short distance away at a spot called Junction Pool. Anglers have been coming to these waters since the nineteenth century, and the tradition of American dry-fly fishing took shape in these valleys, with local fly tyers developing patterns that are still used today. A fly-fishing museum a few miles up the road in Livingston Manor tells the story.

Roscoe also has railroad history. For decades, the New York, Ontario and Western Railway ran trains from the city to the Catskills, carrying holidaymakers and fishermen to the boarding houses and hotels of the Borscht Belt, and Roscoe was a major stop. The railway has gone, but the village keeps a small, workaday look, with a main street of shops, diners and sporting goods stores, and a long-established diner that serves enormous breakfasts. The valley around it is quiet, green and farmed, with hills rising on either side in a pattern of woods and pasture.

Riding here is delightful. Old Route 17, which follows the river through the valley, is a winding road that the interstate has bypassed, and it has light traffic, old bridges and views of the water. Back roads climb into the hills, with steep gradients and tight bends, and the surface is rough in places because of frost heave. In May, when the hatch is on and the dogwood and apple trees are in bloom, the fishermen stand shoulder-deep in the river at dawn, and the whole valley feels like a quiet church. Autumn colour comes in October.

The village has fuel and food, but a larger town is a long way off, since Fallsburg, the nearest place with a significant population, is more than thirty kilometres away. Fill the tank here or in Livingston Manor before heading off into the hills toward the Pepacton Reservoir, where services are few. If you want to try fishing, a licence is needed, and local shops sell flies and give good advice. Mornings are cool even in summer, and a thermos of coffee is a good companion.
t.phoenicia mountain road@42.1,-74.3:
Phoenicia is a small hamlet in the Esopus Creek valley, in the heart of the Catskill Mountains, and it is the point where several of the region's best roads come together. The creek, a fast, clear trout stream, runs right through the village, and in summer, tubers in inner tubes float down it by the hundreds. Hills rise steeply on all sides, thickly wooded with hemlock, maple and beech, and the highest of the Catskills, Slide Mountain, at about 1,270 metres, stands a short way to the south.

The village was once a stop on the Ulster and Delaware Railroad, which carried visitors from the Hudson River to the mountain hotels, and the old station still stands, with a heritage railway running excursions on part of the line. The area was also a centre of bluestone quarrying and leather tanning, trades that stripped the hemlock forests of their bark in the nineteenth century. The forest has regrown and is now protected as part of the Catskill Park, and the creek's water flows into the reservoirs that supply New York City with some of the best drinking water in the world.

For riders, Phoenicia is a crossroads. Route 28 follows the valley to the west toward Margaretville and Pepacton Reservoir, a gentle, flowing road with long curves beside the creek. Route 214 runs north through Stony Clove Notch, a deep, narrow gap between steep mountains, with tight turns, a steep grade and cliffs rising on either side, and it is a real mountain road. Woodstock, an artists' town famous for the music festival that was not actually held there, lies a short ride to the east and has plenty of cafes and shops.

The village has a handful of cafes, including a diner that has become a favourite stop for people driving up from the city, and a few shops. Fuel in the hamlet is limited, so it is wiser to fill the tank in Kingston or Woodstock, the larger towns to the east, or farther along Route 28. Weekends in summer and autumn bring crowds, so go early. In winter the roads can be icy and the notch is slow to clear. In October the colours on the surrounding hills are startling, a deep red and gold that fills the whole valley.
t.crawford notch@44.2,-71.4:
Crawford Notch is a deep gash in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, a glacier-carved, U-shaped valley that squeezes between steep granite walls, with the road, a railway line and the headwaters of the Saco River all running through the gap at about 580 metres. The cliffs on either side rise hundreds of metres, streaked with waterfalls, and the whole setting has a drama unusual for the eastern United States. US 302 runs through the notch, a well-surfaced road with gentle gradients and moderate curves, and it is among the most scenic in New England.

The valley has a tragic story. In August 1826, after a night of torrential rain, a landslide roared down the mountain above a lonely house belonging to the Willey family, and nine people, the parents, their children and hired men, were killed trying to flee. The house itself was spared, split by the slide, and the story shocked the country and made the notch famous. Writers such as Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote about it, and the site is now a small state historic site with a little museum. The Crawford Path, cut up Mount Washington from near the head of the notch in 1819, is among the oldest hiking trails in the country.

The railway adds to the drama. The Maine Central line through the notch, completed in the 1870s after enormous effort, crosses the Frankenstein Trestle, a high iron bridge named after a local landscape painter, and a scenic train runs along it in summer and autumn. From the road, you can see the trestle spanning the gully. Waterfalls such as Silver Cascade, which drops beside the road in a series of steps, are worth a short stop, and there are trailheads for many hikes. The big hotel at Bretton Woods, built in 1902, was the venue for the monetary conference that set up the post-war international financial system.

Moose are common on this road, especially at dawn and dusk, and a collision with one is a serious hazard, so ride with care. Weather can be sudden, with fog, rain and cold even in summer. Fuel is not available in the notch itself; look in Bartlett or Conway to the south, or in Twin Mountain to the north. Foliage season in early October brings heavy traffic, but the colours on the hillsides are superb. Pack a warm layer, because the valley is cool and the shade of the cliffs deep.
t.rockport@42.7,-70.6:
Rockport sits at the tip of Cape Ann, on the Massachusetts coast north of Boston, and it is a town that lives by granite and by its looks. A red fishing shack on a wharf in the harbour, known as Motif Number 1, has been painted and photographed by so many artists that it is often called the most painted building in America, and a visit to the quay at dawn, with fishing boats and lobster pots in the light, shows why. The town's streets are lined with galleries and shops, and a stone breakwater curves out into the water.

The rock under your feet explains the town. Cape Ann is made of tough grey granite, and from the early nineteenth century the quarries here supplied stone for buildings, bridges and paving blocks across the country, with ships carrying it to Boston and New York. The workings are now flooded, forming deep green pools, and the big one at Halibut Point State Park can be reached by a short walk. The park has a ledge of granite sloping to the sea, where waves crash and gulls wheel, and on a clear day you can see the coast of New Hampshire and the Isles of Shoals.

Offshore, Thacher Island carries twin lighthouses, built in the 1860s, which can be seen from the shore and visited by boat in season. Rockport's narrow streets, especially around Bearskin Neck, a spit of land jammed with shops, restaurants and old fishing sheds, are charming but crowded, and the summer weekends are almost impossible. The roads to town, Route 127 and Route 127A, wind through woods and past stone walls, with glimpses of the sea, and they are narrow, twisty and slow.

Gloucester, six kilometres away, has the fuel stations and larger supermarkets, along with a famous fishing fleet and a memorial to fishermen lost at sea. Rockport has small shops, and a lobster roll at a harbourside shack is the traditional meal. Fog is common on this coast, and the air is cool even in July, so bring a layer. October is a lovely month, with the crowds gone and the autumn light on the water. If you can, stay for sunset.
t.brewster@41.8,-70.1:
Brewster lies on the northern shore of Cape Cod, along the Cape Cod Bay side, where the tide goes out so far that the flats stretch for a mile or more, leaving a vast expanse of wet, rippled sand dotted with seabirds and people digging for clams. At low tide, you can walk a long way out toward the water, and at high tide, the bay fills quickly, so the locals check the tables. The town is quiet, wooded and relaxed, and the main road through it, Route 6A, is one of the loveliest in the region.

Route 6A, the Old King's Highway, follows the old track along the bay side of the Cape, and it is preserved as a historic district, with a ban on billboards and strict rules on new buildings. The road is lined with antique shops, galleries, old inns and white clapboard houses, with sea captains' mansions among them. In the nineteenth century, Brewster was home to dozens of sea captains, who sailed the world and brought back goods and fortune. The town's old general store has been selling penny candy and groceries for more than a century.

Inland, the landscape is a product of the glaciers. Nickerson State Park, a large area of pine forest and freshwater ponds, sits among kettle holes, depressions left when great blocks of ice melted and left deep ponds, and it has camping, swimming and miles of bike trails. The Cape Cod Rail Trail, a paved path along an old railway, passes through the park. At Stony Brook, in spring, you can watch herring swimming up a series of steps beside a restored mill, a spectacle that draws crowds in April and May.

For riders, the Cape is slow but charming, with 6A a gentle road that bends past old houses and marshes, though traffic in summer can be heavy and the speed limit low. Early morning is the best time. Harwich, about eight kilometres away, and Orleans have fuel stations and shops, and Brewster itself has a few restaurants and cafes serving chowder, fried clams and ice cream. Sea breezes keep the temperature moderate, and fog can roll in. Autumn is excellent, with warm days, cool nights and empty roads.
t.cohasset@42.2,-70.8:
Cohasset is where Boston's South Shore turns rocky. Most of the coast between the city and Plymouth is low and sandy, but here the granite pushes up through the turf, and the road along the water, Route 3A, winds past stone walls, big old trees and views of a harbour full of moored sailboats. The village green, with its white church and Victorian town hall, looks like a stage set, and the whole place has a polished, unhurried air.

The sea off Cohasset has claimed more than its share of ships. A mile or so offshore, Minot's Ledge is a reef that shows only at low tide, and the first lighthouse built on it, an iron tower on spindly legs, was swept away in a great storm in April 1851 with two assistant keepers inside. The replacement, an immense tower of interlocking granite blocks, was finished in 1860 and still stands, a stern grey pillar rising out of the waves. Its light flashes in a pattern of one, four and three, which sailors and lovers translate as I love you, and the tower is known locally by that name.

Another disaster is remembered here, too. In October 1849, the brig St John, carrying Irish families fleeing the famine, wrecked on the rocks in a gale within sight of the shore, and nearly a hundred people drowned. The town buried the dead, and a memorial, with a moving sculpture, now stands near the harbour. Cohasset's history of wreckage, rescue and quiet remembrance gives the pleasant seafront a sombre depth.

For a rider, the coast road is slow and lovely, with tight bends between stone walls, a speed limit that is enforced and plenty of cyclists in good weather. Beyond the village, the road runs along the edge of the marshes to Scituate and Marshfield, with the Atlantic glinting beyond. Traffic is light on weekday mornings and heavier at weekends. The surface is mostly good, though frost heaves can roughen the edges in spring. Fog rolls in from the sea at any time and drops the temperature sharply.

With about seven thousand people, Cohasset has fuel and the basics, and a few cafes and seafood places around the harbour and the common, but if you want a wider choice, Hingham, a short way to the northwest, and Scituate to the south are both easy. A coffee and a blueberry muffin on the harbour wall is a good start, and a lobster roll at a harbourside shack makes a fine lunch. In autumn, the light over the water is superb, with a low gold glow that turns the granite pink. Take a moment at the memorial before you go.
t.scituate@42.2,-70.7:
Scituate is a harbour town on the South Shore with two stories that people there tell with relish. The first concerns the War of 1812. In September 1814, a British warship was cruising off the coast, and two young sisters, Rebecca and Abigail Bates, who were alone in the lighthouse keeper's house while their father was away, are said to have grabbed a drum and a fife and hidden behind the dunes, playing as loudly as they could. The British, believing a company of militia was approaching, turned back. The story has been told so often that the sisters are known as the Army of Two, and the little lighthouse, built in 1811 on Cedar Point, is one of the oldest on the coast.

The second story is about seaweed. For more than a century, Scituate was the centre of Irish moss harvesting, a red seaweed that was raked from the rocks at low tide, dried in the sun and sold for use as a thickener in food, and the trade made a modest living for many local families. A small museum on the harbour tells the story of the moss gatherers, along with the fishermen and the shipbuilders. The harbour itself is busy and full of life, with lobster boats, draggers and pleasure craft, and a row of seafood restaurants and shops along the quay.

The coast here is flat and exposed, and the town has paid for it. Winter storms, especially nor'easters, have repeatedly overtopped the sea walls and flooded streets, and the blizzard of 1978 is still remembered for the damage it caused. Beaches such as Minot and Humarock have been rebuilt time and again. In summer, the water is cold but clear, and the long sandy shore at Peggotty Beach is popular with walkers and families. A walk out along the breakwater to the lighthouse is a pleasant half-hour, with views across Massachusetts Bay.

For riders, the roads along the South Shore are slow, narrow and winding, with Route 3A running along the coast and a mix of side roads through old farmland and marshes. Traffic is moderate, heavy on summer weekends. Scituate has five thousand residents and no shortage of stations, bakeries and pubs, so refuelling and a bite to eat are easy. Fresh fish and chips, fried clams and chowder are everywhere, and Irish pubs are plentiful in this heavily Irish-American region. Sea fog can be thick in spring and early summer, and the wind is sharp. The sunsets are worth waiting for.
t.lanesborough@42.5,-73.2:
Lanesborough sits at the foot of the Berkshire Hills in the far west of Massachusetts, at about 350 metres, in the broad valley of the Hoosic River, with the great bulk of Mount Greylock to the east. At 1,064 metres, Greylock is the highest peak in the state, a broad, forested massif that dominates the skyline for miles, and a ride to its summit is the main reason for coming here. The town itself is a quiet, rural place of farms, old white houses and a lake, Pontoosuc, that fills with boats in summer.

The mountain has a literary pedigree. Herman Melville lived at a farm near Pittsfield, and he wrote Moby-Dick in a study that looked out toward Greylock, whose long, humped outline is said to have suggested the shape of the white whale. He dedicated a later book to the mountain. The summit is crowned by the Veterans War Memorial Tower, a tall granite lighthouse-like structure built in the 1930s, and the view from the top on a clear day reaches into five states, with the Catskills, the Green Mountains and the Taconics laid out below.

The road to the top, the Mount Greylock Scenic Byway, is a narrow, winding mountain road with fine surfaces, tight bends and long climbs, and it takes about forty minutes to ride at a leisurely pace. It passes through forests of northern hardwood and spruce, with the smell of balsam and damp earth, and the temperature at the summit can be fifteen degrees cooler than in the valley. The road is closed in winter, usually from late autumn to mid-May, so check before you set out. In October, the maples blaze and the road is crowded.

Fuel is available in Lanesborough, a small town, and in Pittsfield, a few kilometres south, which has a full range of services, and in Dalton, whose paper mill has made the paper for American banknotes for generations. Bring a layer for the summit, and expect fog and wind. Black bears live on the mountain, and so do moose, so keep an eye on the verges. The Appalachian Trail passes over the summit, and hikers with huge packs are a common sight. A cup of tea in the lodge at the top, with the whole of the Berkshires below, is a quiet pleasure.
t.hanover@43.7,-72.3:
Hanover is a town that exists around a college, and you feel it the moment you roll in. Dartmouth, founded in 1769 by Eleazar Wheelock to educate Native American students and the sons of colonists, owns the centre of the place, a long, broad green surrounded by white clapboard and red brick. The Appalachian Trail runs straight along Main Street here, so it is common to see hikers with muddy boots and heavy packs buying sandwiches next to students in fleece. Theodor Geisel, who became Dr. Seuss, studied here and edited the humour magazine.

The town sits on the New Hampshire bank of the Connecticut River, with Vermont just across the Ledyard Bridge in Norwich. The river valley is wide, quiet and farmed, a green trough between the White Mountains to the east and the Green Mountains to the west. A few kilometres south, Lebanon and West Lebanon hold the bigger stores and gas stations, while Hanover itself has cafes, a food co-op and bookshops that make it a good place to start a morning. Fuel is limited within the tight centre, so fill up in Lebanon if you can.

Riding north on Route 10, the road runs just above the river through farmland and old villages, with long views across to Vermont. The surface is generally good, the corners relaxed, and the speed limits are steady. In autumn, the maples go a violent red and gold, and the road becomes busy with leaf-watchers, so a weekday is kinder. Spring brings mud and frost heaves, while summer is warm and green, with swimming holes on the river.

The area is steeped in New England character, with stone walls, covered bridges and stately town greens. Sugar maple sap boils into syrup in March, and the smell of woodsmoke hangs in the valley. Take time for a walk across the green and a look at the old college buildings. Then head north, because the best of the river road lies ahead.
t.franconia notch@44.2,-71.7:
Franconia Notch is a gap in the White Mountains where a glacier once scoured a deep trough, leaving granite walls rising steeply on either side. The notch is about eight miles long, with Cannon Mountain on the west and the Kinsman and Franconia ranges on the east, and the road threads through the bottom at around 1,900 feet. The ridge above is bare rock and spruce, and the sound of wind in the trees carries down to the highway. For years the main attraction was the Old Man of the Mountain, a natural profile on a cliff face that appeared on the state's licence plates and quarter, until it collapsed in May 2003. A memorial of steel rods and plaques on the lake shore now shows where it once hung.

Today there are other draws. The Flume Gorge, a narrow ravine of moss-covered granite with a boardwalk, is a short walk from the visitor centre. Echo Lake lies at the northern end beneath Cannon's cliff, and the Cannon Mountain Aerial Tramway, the first in North America when it opened in 1938, lifts passengers to the summit for a wide view over New Hampshire and across to the Green Mountains of Vermont on a clear day. The Appalachian Trail passes nearby, and the Pemigewasset River rises close to the road.

Riding here is an unusual experience, since the route is part of Interstate 93 but is built as a parkway, a two-lane road with a low speed limit and no passing in places. It is a scenic, slow ride, with granite on both sides and trees flaming in autumn. The surface is smooth, but frost can linger in shade in spring and autumn, and the notch is often cooler and damper than the valleys. Fog and rain are common, and the best light is in the morning.

Lincoln, to the south, has fuel and food, and Franconia and Littleton lie to the north, with more services. Parking at the main sites is paid, and lots fill up by mid-morning in the peak season, so come early. October brings leaf-watchers by the thousand, so a weekday visit is kinder.
t.palisades parkway north@40.9,-73.9:
Riverdale sits at the northern tip of the Bronx, where New York City presses up against the Hudson and the Palisades rise across the water, and it is probably the greenest and quietest corner of the borough. Big old houses sit on a ridge above the river, and the Henry Hudson Parkway runs along the shore, an elegant, curving road from the 1930s built to give city families a pleasant drive.

The area has a long literary and artistic history. Wave Hill, a public garden and cultural centre on an old estate above the river, has hosted guests including Mark Twain, who rented it in the early 1900s, and Theodore Roosevelt, who spent summers there as a boy. The gardens, with their long views across to the Palisades, are among the best in the city. A short way south, Spuyten Duyvil, where the Harlem River meets the Hudson, is a handsome bit of water with a railway bridge and an old Dutch name that translates, so the story goes, as spitting devil.

For the rider, the thing to know is that this is the gateway. The Henry Hudson Parkway north leads onto the Saw Mill and then the roads into Westchester, and the way across the George Washington Bridge to the Palisades Parkway is a short ride south. Traffic in this part of the Bronx can be heavy, and the parkway has low bridges and tight curves that are no place for hurry. Early on a weekend morning, though, the river light is wonderful.

Autumn brings gold and red to the park trees, while summer afternoons are humid and hazy. Take a few minutes at the river overlook before you set off.
t.storm king highway@41.4,-74.0:

t.guatavita@4.9,-73.8:

t.yarmouth port@41.7,-70.2:

t.dennis@41.7,-70.2:

t.pittsfield@42.5,-73.2:

t.lenox@42.4,-73.3:

t.new salem@42.5,-72.3:

t.ashfield@42.5,-72.8:

t.sagamore@41.8,-70.5:

t.patapampa pass@-15.7,-71.5:

t.cruz del condor@-15.6,-71.9:

t.kancamagus pass@44.0,-71.5:

t.hairpin turn@42.7,-73.1:

t.hunter mountain edge@42.2,-74.2:

t.phoenicia@42.1,-74.3:

t.guasca@4.9,-73.9:

t.quabbin park@42.3,-72.3:
Quabbin Reservoir is a drowned valley, and the quiet around it comes partly from that. t.northbridge@42.2,-71.6:

t.dover@42.2,-71.3:

t.sherborn@42.2,-71.4:

t.wachusett mountain@42.5,-71.9:

t.westminster@42.5,-71.9:

t.clinton@42.4,-71.7:

t.plum island@42.8,-70.8:

t.ipswich@42.7,-70.8:

t.conway@42.5,-72.7:

t.searsburg@42.9,-73.0:

t.wilmington@42.9,-72.9:

t.west dover@42.9,-72.8:

t.middlesex fells@42.4,-71.1:

t.winchester@42.5,-71.1:

t.westborough@42.3,-71.6:

t.northborough@42.3,-71.6:

t.west barnstable@41.7,-70.4:

t.annisquam@42.7,-70.7:

t.pigeon cove@42.7,-70.6:

t.rockwell road@42.6,-73.2:

t.beverly@42.6,-70.9:

t.magnolia@42.6,-70.7:

t.point judith@41.4,-71.5:

t.ocean drive@41.5,-71.3:

t.cornwall bridge@41.8,-73.4:

t.sharon@41.9,-73.5:

t.lakeville@42.0,-73.4:

t.smugglers notch@44.5,-72.8:
Smugglers' Notch earns its name honestly. t.williamstown@42.7,-73.2:

t.north adams@42.7,-73.1:

t.boston@42.4,-71.1:

t.central@-45.1,169.1:

t.hawk s nest@40.8,-73.7:

t.adirondack@41.0,-74.3:

t.lincoln new hampshire@44.0,-71.7:

t.tarrytown croton@40.7,-73.6:

t.berkshires mohawk@40.6,-74.2:

t.catskills@40.9,-73.8:

t.vermont green@40.6,-74.3:

t.jersey highlands@40.7,-74.4:

t.north@40.9,-74.4:

t.brattleboro@42.9,-72.6:

t.hudson highlands@40.8,-73.6:

t.salem@42.5,-70.9:

t.greenfield@42.6,-72.6:

t.great barrington@42.2,-73.4:

t.belchertown@42.3,-72.4:

t.northampton@42.3,-72.6:

t.plymouth@42.0,-70.7:

t.newport@41.5,-71.3:

t.pawtucket@41.9,-71.4:

t.kent@41.7,-73.5:

t.gorham@44.4,-71.2:

t.waterbury@44.3,-72.8:

t.litchfield hills@40.6,-74.1:

t.st johnsbury@44.4,-72.0:

t.deerfield@44.2,-71.6:

t.sterling@42.4,-71.8:

t.harvard@42.5,-71.6:

t.concord@42.5,-71.3:

t.tiverton@41.6,-71.2:

Carmel has fuel, delis, pizza places and coffee shops. Mahopac and Brewster, just nearby, have more shops and restaurants. On the way back to the city, the Taconic State Parkway is the scenic route south, though traffic builds in the evening as you approach Westchester.
t.sea girt@40.1,-74.0:
A short red-brick lighthouse with a square tower stands on the corner of Ocean Avenue in Sea Girt, looking more like a Victorian house that grew a lantern than a proper beacon. It was built in the 1890s to fill a dark gap in the chain of lights along the Jersey Shore, and today volunteers keep it open for occasional tours. Around it, Sea Girt is a small, quiet, well-kept borough of shingled houses, wide lawns and shady streets, with a non-commercial boardwalk running along a clean, broad beach.

That lack of commerce is the town's whole character. There are no arcades or amusement piers here, unlike some of the louder resort towns up and down the coast. Families come for the sand and the sea, and the main excitement is an ice cream from the next town. The New Jersey National Guard has a large training centre on the edge of town, and the state's governors once used a summer residence on its grounds, which gave the place a certain political glamour in the early twentieth century.

The swim is straightforward: Atlantic surf, sandy bottom, lifeguards in season and generally clean water. In summer you need a daily or seasonal beach badge, as almost everywhere on the Jersey Shore, which you can buy at the beach entrances. The water warms through July and August to a comfortable temperature, though early in summer it can still be bracing. Watch for rip currents on rough days and swim between the flags.

Riding here is gentle. Route 71 and Ocean Avenue run along the coast between Spring Lake and Manasquan, with old houses, small lakes and the sea always close by. Traffic is slow in summer, with pedestrians and cyclists everywhere, and parking can be tricky near the beach, but a motorcycle squeezes in where cars cannot. Manasquan, just south, has the inlet where fishing boats head out to sea, and a busy strip of beach bars and seafood places.

Fuel and food are close at hand in Manasquan and along Route 71. On a hot summer day, a swim in the surf and a lazy hour on the sand are just the thing before heading north again toward the Hudson Valley and the next leg of the ride.
t.throgs neck@40.8,-73.8:
The Throgs Neck Bridge lands on a peninsula at the far southeastern corner of the Bronx, and from the water's edge here you look out over the place where the East River widens into Long Island Sound. The neighbourhood of Throgs Neck itself is a quiet, low-rise part of the city, a mix of small houses, waterfront bungalows, churches and corner delis, where it is easy to forget you are in New York City at all. The name comes from John Throckmorton, an early settler of the 1640s, worn down over the centuries into its current form.

At the tip of the peninsula stands Fort Schuyler, a granite fort built in the nineteenth century to guard the eastern approach to New York Harbor. It now houses the State University of New York Maritime College, and a training ship is often moored alongside. Across the water, the Throgs Neck Bridge and the Bronx–Whitestone Bridge cross to Queens, and on a clear evening the sunsets over the water, with the bridges silhouetted, are very fine.

The swim, though, needs honesty. The waters around the neck are tidal, with strong currents and boat traffic, and there are no lifeguarded public beaches on the peninsula itself; some waterfront communities have small private beaches for residents. The city's proper swimming beach is Orchard Beach in Pelham Bay Park, a few kilometres north, a long, curving crescent of sand built in the 1930s, with lifeguards and facilities in summer. That is where to head if you want to get wet.

The riding into Throgs Neck is all city: the Cross Bronx Expressway, the Throgs Neck Expressway and the Bruckner, with heavy traffic, potholes, aggressive drivers and constant construction. The bridges charge tolls collected electronically, so make sure your plate is registered or expect a bill by mail. Once off the highways, the local streets are calm and easy.

There are fuel stations, delis, pizza places and diners close by on East Tremont and Throgs Neck boulevards. After a long ride from the Berkshires and the Mohawk Trail, with their hill farms and covered bridges, sitting on a bench by the water and watching the boats go under the bridge is a satisfying way to come back to the city.
t.near hardwick on the way back@41.0,-74.9:
Up here in Warren County, in the northwestern corner of New Jersey, the long, straight crest of the Kittatinny Ridge runs along the horizon, and beyond it lies the Delaware River and the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area. Hardwick is a rural township of farms, forest and small lakes in the valley just east of the ridge, and it feels a world away from the crowded state most people imagine.

The ridge is a single long fold of hard sandstone and conglomerate that stretches for hundreds of kilometres through Pennsylvania and New Jersey into New York, and the Appalachian Trail runs along its top. At the Delaware Water Gap, the river cuts straight through it in a spectacular gorge. Inside the recreation area, the Old Mine Road, one of the oldest roads in the United States, follows the river past abandoned farms and the restored village of Millbrook, a small cluster of nineteenth-century buildings preserved as a living museum. Nearby Blairstown was the location for the original Friday the 13th film, and its old main street and the camp setting are still recognised by horror fans.

For a swim, the clearest nearby option is Swartswood Lake, in a state park near Newton, with a public beach and lifeguards in summer. The Delaware River also has some popular swimming and tubing spots, but the current can be deceptive and drownings happen every year, so stick to guarded areas. On hot days the lakes of this area fill with families, and the water is warm and clean by midsummer.

The roads are a delight. Small county routes twist through the valley, past dairy farms and woods, over low hills and along streams, with very little traffic on weekdays. Old Mine Road itself is narrow and uneven, with tight bends and occasional gravel, and sections have been closed at times for repairs, so check before you go. Watch for deer, tractors, and cyclists.

Fuel and food are a bit thin out here. Blairstown and Newton, about twelve kilometres away, are the nearest towns with stations, supermarkets and cafes. On the way back east, the run through Sussex County to the highways is pretty and gradual, with fields and forest giving way slowly to the suburbs.
t.edgewater@40.8,-74.0:
Edgewater is a thin ribbon of a town squeezed between the Hudson River and the foot of the Palisades, the dark basalt cliffs that line the New Jersey side of the river opposite Manhattan. Across the water, so close it almost looks touchable, lies the Upper West Side, with Riverside Park, the tower of Riverside Church and Grant's Tomb visible above the trees.

The Palisades are what make this place. They formed some two hundred million years ago when molten rock pushed up into layers of sediment and cooled into tall columns, and they rise up to a hundred and fifty metres above the river. In the nineteenth century, quarrymen were blasting them apart for building stone and gravel, until a campaign by conservation groups and wealthy patrons led to the creation of the Palisades Interstate Park in the early twentieth century, one of the first parks of its kind in America.

Edgewater itself was once industrial, with factories, a Ford assembly plant and docks along the river. Most of that has gone, replaced by apartment towers, shopping centres and a waterfront walkway with views over the river. There is a large Japanese shopping complex here, a favourite of the region's Japanese community, where you can eat noodles and sushi after a long day.

The riding into Edgewater is short but special. River Road follows the base of the cliffs along the Hudson, a winding road with views of Manhattan opening between the buildings. Up on top, Palisades Avenue and the Palisades Interstate Parkway run along the cliff tops through forest, and scenic overlooks give tremendous views across to Manhattan and up the river. Traffic is heavy on weekdays, and approaching the George Washington Bridge, just north in Fort Lee, can be painful at rush hour.

Tanks, sandwiches and espresso are all a few blocks away. After a ride all the way from Montauk at the eastern tip of Long Island, or through the Catskill high peaks, finishing here, with the whole length of Manhattan glittering across the river in the evening, is a fitting end to a long day on the bike.
t.near manville on the way back@40.5,-74.6:
Manville takes its name from a factory. In the early twentieth century, the Johns-Manville company built a huge plant here in central New Jersey, producing asbestos building materials, and a town grew around it to house the workers, many of them immigrants from Eastern Europe. The plant closed in the 1980s after asbestos was found to be deadly, and the company was bankrupted by lawsuits. Today Manville is a modest working-class borough of small houses and shops, sitting where the Raritan and Millstone rivers meet.

Those rivers are both a blessing and a curse. Manville lies low, and it has flooded badly many times, most recently in 2021, when the remnants of Hurricane Ida sent water through the streets. Along the Millstone, the Delaware and Raritan Canal, dug in the 1830s to carry coal and goods between the Delaware River and New York, runs past quiet towpaths shaded by trees, now a long state park popular with walkers and cyclists. Nearby in Hillsborough, Duke Farms, the former estate of the tobacco heiress Doris Duke, is open to the public as a nature reserve with meadows, woods and lakes.

The swim needs a caveat. The Raritan and Millstone are not great swimming rivers; they are slow, muddy and can carry runoff after rain, and the canal is off-limits. If you want a dip, the better option is a public lake or a pool elsewhere, or the beaches of the Shore further south and east. Here, a cold drink in the shade by the canal may be the more sensible way to cool off.

Riding around Manville is mostly flat and suburban, with county roads crossing farmland and housing between the rivers. To the west and north, though, the land rises into the Sourland Mountains and the hills toward Somerset and Hunterdon counties, where the roads become more interesting, twisting through forest and past old farms and villages. Watch for deer, potholes and slow traffic around the towns.

Manville and the surrounding towns have fuel, delis, pizza and diners. Heading back toward New York means along Route 206, Route 22 and the busy highways of central New Jersey, which fill with traffic at rush hour.
t.east elmhurst@40.8,-73.9:
Planes are the soundtrack of East Elmhurst. The neighbourhood sits on the northern edge of Queens, right beside LaGuardia Airport, and jets come in low over the rooftops toward the runways along Flushing Bay all day long. It is a residential area of row houses and small apartment buildings, with a long history as a middle-class African American neighbourhood and more recently a destination for Latin American and other immigrant families.

Malcolm X lived here in the 1960s, and his house in East Elmhurst was firebombed in February 1965, just a week before he was assassinated in Manhattan. Not far away in Corona, the jazz trumpeter Louis Armstrong lived in a modest brick house for nearly thirty years until his death in 1971, and it is now a museum with his furniture, records and recordings of his voice. Flushing Meadows–Corona Park, a little to the southeast, hosted two World's Fairs, and the giant steel globe called the Unisphere still stands there, along with the tennis stadiums of the US Open.

Riding in is all about traffic. The Grand Central Parkway, the Brooklyn–Queens Expressway and the approach roads to the airport are among the busiest in the city, with tight merges, potholes, sudden lane changes and taxis jostling for space. After the open roads of Vermont and the Berkshires, the density can be a shock. Keep your wits about you, cover the brake, and do not expect anyone to leave space.

The reward is food. Jackson Heights, right next door, is one of the most diverse neighbourhoods in the world, and its streets are lined with restaurants serving Indian, Nepali, Tibetan, Colombian, Mexican, Ecuadorian and Thai food, among many others. You can eat momos, arepas and tacos within a few blocks. Fuel is easy to find on Astoria Boulevard and Northern Boulevard.

For an evening view, ride a few minutes to the waterfront along Flushing Bay, where a promenade looks out over the boats and the airport runways, and watch the planes landing against the Manhattan skyline as the lights come on.
t.near newark@40.7,-74.2:
Newark is New Jersey's biggest city and one of the oldest in the United States, founded by Puritans from Connecticut in 1666. It grew into an industrial powerhouse, making leather, beer, jewellery and much more, then suffered badly in the decline of the late twentieth century, including the riots of 1967. Today it is a city of contrasts: a business district of office towers, a major university and arts centre, airport and port, and neighbourhoods that are still recovering.

This finish lies near the Passaic River, close to the Ironbound district, so called because it was hemmed in by railway lines. The Ironbound has long been a Portuguese and Brazilian neighbourhood, and its streets, especially Ferry Street, are packed with restaurants serving grilled meats, salt cod, seafood rice and enormous portions at reasonable prices. After a long day in the saddle, a plate of grilled chicken and a cold beer here is about as good an ending as you can get.

Across town, Branch Brook Park has one of the largest collections of cherry trees in the country, which bloom in spectacular pink in April, and the Newark Museum of Art holds an excellent collection. Newark's Prudential Center hosts hockey and concerts, and the city's Penn Station is a handsome 1930s building.

The roads into Newark are among the busiest in the country. The New Jersey Turnpike, Route 1&9, Route 21 and Interstate 280 all converge here, with heavy trucks heading to the port and airport, constant construction and complex junctions. Potholes are common. Ride defensively and expect to sit in traffic at peak hours. Remember that in New Jersey an attendant fills your tank for you.

Fuel, food and every service are close by. If you want to see something before calling it a day, the riverfront park along the Passaic in the Ironbound is a pleasant spot to stretch out, with views of the bridges and the city skyline. Behind you lie the hills and forests of the Berkshires and Vermont, and for all its grit, Newark makes a lively and well-fed place to roll in at the end.
t.mott haven@40.8,-73.9:
The southernmost tip of the Bronx is where Mott Haven and Port Morris meet the Harlem and East rivers, a grid of brick tenements, warehouses, rail yards and highway viaducts just across the water from Manhattan and Randall's Island. The area takes its name from Jordan Mott, an inventor who opened an iron works here in the 1840s, and the factories that followed made the South Bronx an industrial district for generations.

Mott Haven became a symbol of urban decline in the 1970s, when fires and abandonment swept through the South Bronx, and it was also part of the borough where hip hop was born at block parties of that era. Today it is changing fast, with new apartment buildings, galleries and restaurants along the waterfront, while many long-time residents worry about rising rents. The historic district around Alexander Avenue has handsome rows of nineteenth-century brownstones and churches, and the streets have a lively, Latin flavour, with music, bodegas and food carts.

The riding in is pure city. The Major Deegan Expressway, the Bruckner and the approaches to the Third Avenue, Willis Avenue and Triborough bridges cross here in a tangle of ramps and viaducts, with heavy trucks heading to the markets at Hunts Point, potholes, and fast lane changes. Some bridges are free and others charge tolls, collected electronically. It is noisy and hectic, and after a day in the Appalachian hills or the Catskill gorges it will feel like riding into a beehive.

Fuel, food and coffee are easy to find, and the neighbourhood's restaurants serve Puerto Rican, Dominican and Mexican food at fair prices. A plate of rice, beans and roast pork is the right meal after a long ride.

To clear your head before parking up, Randall's Island is just across a footbridge or a short ride away, with parks, sports fields and paths along the river where you can watch the sun set behind Manhattan. From here, every route into the city or home is close, and you have the satisfaction of having ridden from the mountains to the middle of one of the world's great cities in a single day.
t.monmouth beach@40.3,-74.0:
Between the ocean and the Shrewsbury River lies a strip of land so thin that in places you can see water on both sides of the road, and Monmouth Beach occupies a stretch of it. It is a small, wealthy borough just north of Long Branch, with large homes facing the river, a marina, and an ocean beach protected by a massive stone sea wall that runs for kilometres along this part of the coast.

The sea wall is the story of this coast. Without it, storms would long ago have washed away the narrow barrier, and the towns along Ocean Avenue between Long Branch and Sea Bright have been battered many times, most memorably in 2012, when Hurricane Sandy breached the dunes and flooded houses. Behind the wall and the dunes, the beaches have been rebuilt with sand pumped from offshore, and they are wide and clean in summer.

To the north lies Sandy Hook, a long sandy spit reaching toward New York Harbor, part of the Gateway National Recreation Area. It has beaches, maritime forest, the old military buildings of Fort Hancock, and the Sandy Hook Lighthouse, built in 1764 and the oldest working lighthouse in the United States. On a clear day, the Manhattan skyline is visible across the water from the northern tip.

For a swim, the ocean beaches here and at Sandy Hook are good, with lifeguards in summer, though Monmouth Beach's own beach is controlled by a beach club and badges are required. Sandy Hook's public beaches are the easier option, with a parking fee in season. The water warms through the summer, and on a hot day there is nothing better than a plunge in the surf.

Riding along Ocean Avenue is a pleasure: the sea wall on one side, the river and big houses on the other, and the road rolling north toward Sea Bright and the Highlands, where a tall bridge crosses the Shrewsbury and the land rises sharply. Traffic is heavy on summer weekends. Long Branch, three kilometres south, has fuel, food and every service, and the start and finish of a Finger Lakes overnight here means a long run north, so fill up and set off early.
t.concord@40.6,-74.1:
The Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge fills the sky over this part of Staten Island. Concord is a residential neighbourhood on the island's eastern side, a few streets back from the water and just inland from the bridge, a quiet mix of detached houses, small apartment blocks, churches and corner shops. When the bridge opened in 1964 it was the longest suspension span in the world, and it changed Staten Island forever, linking it by road to Brooklyn and turning a semi-rural borough into a commuter suburb almost overnight.

Close by, at the foot of the bridge, Fort Wadsworth has guarded the Narrows, the entrance to New York Harbor, since colonial times, and its stone batteries and grassy ramparts offer one of the best views anywhere of the bridge, the harbour and the towers of Lower Manhattan beyond. In neighbouring Rosebank, the Alice Austen House, a small cottage on the water, was home to one of America's first notable women photographers, and her pictures of nineteenth-century New York life are displayed inside.

Riding onto Staten Island means tolls and traffic. The Verrazzano charges a steep toll in one direction, and the Staten Island Expressway can be slow at almost any hour. Local streets are a mix of smooth tarmac, patches and potholes, with buses, delivery trucks and double-parked cars. For the scenic way in, Hylan Boulevard and the roads along the eastern shore pass beaches, boardwalks and old waterfront houses.

Concord has fuel, delis and pizza places, and Staten Island is justly proud of its pizza and Italian bakeries. If you have time, ride a few minutes north to St. George and take the free Staten Island Ferry across the harbour on foot, past the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island to Lower Manhattan, then back. It is one of the best free experiences in the city.

You arrive here after the Hudson Highlands, where the river cuts through the mountains past Storm King and Bear Mountain, and the contrast is satisfying: from steep forested gorges to the mouth of the same river opening into the sea, with the great bridge striding across it.
t.kearny@40.8,-74.1:
Kearny is a Scottish town that happens to be in New Jersey. In the late nineteenth century, thread mills and linoleum factories run by Scottish companies drew workers from Scotland and Northern Ireland to this hilly strip of land between the Passaic and Hackensack rivers, and they brought with them their churches, pipe bands and, above all, football. For decades Kearny was known as Soccer Town USA, producing an unusual number of players for the US national team, and the sport still matters here more than in most American towns.

The town sits on a ridge above the Meadowlands, with Newark across the Passaic to the west and the Hackensack marshes and Manhattan skyline to the east. The streets near the main avenue still have the feel of an old mill town, with modest brick houses, pubs, bakeries and churches, though many of today's residents are of Portuguese, Latin American and other heritage. Down on the marshes, the old industrial land of Kearny Point and South Kearny is a world of warehouses, rail lines, truck terminals and power lines, crossed by elevated highways.

The riding in is honest urban work. The New Jersey Turnpike, Route 280, the Belleville Pike and Route 7 all cross the area, along with a web of local roads, and trucks are everywhere because of the nearby port and rail yards. Expect potholes, construction and heavy traffic at peak hours. It is not scenic, but crossing the Meadowlands on the elevated roads gives you big views of the marshes, the rivers and the skyline, especially at dusk.

Kearny Avenue has stations, bakeries and coffee, and New Jersey's full-service law means an attendant will fill your tank. If you want a taste of the town's heritage, look for a shop selling Scottish meat pies, sausage rolls and shortbread, a local tradition that has outlived the mills.

After the North Fork of Long Island, with its lighthouses, vineyards and farm stands, or the gentle Litchfield Hills of Connecticut, this finish feels very different, but it has its own story, and the light over the Meadowlands at sunset can be beautiful.
t.north arlington@40.8,-74.1:
North Arlington is a small Bergen County borough perched on a ridge above the Passaic River, with views west toward Belleville and Newark and east over the Meadowlands to the Manhattan skyline. It is a quiet, residential place of small houses, churches and neighbourhood businesses, and much of its land is taken up by large cemeteries, including Holy Cross, one of the biggest Catholic cemeteries in the region.

Its most surprising claim to fame lies underground. In the eighteenth century, the Schuyler family worked a copper mine here, and in the 1750s they installed a steam engine to pump water out of the shafts, the first steam engine in North America, brought over in parts from England. The mine has long since closed, and little remains to see, but local history enthusiasts remember it as the start of the industrial age in America.

The riding into North Arlington is all suburban and urban, along the Passaic River on Riverside Avenue, along Ridge Road and across the busy junctions with Route 7 and Route 17. The roads are lined with shops, houses and traffic lights, with potholes and patches, and traffic can be heavy at rush hour. The Belleville Turnpike crosses the Meadowlands toward Kearny and gives open views of the marshes and the city.

Fuel and food are easy to find along Ridge Road and nearby in Lyndhurst and Belleville. The area has good Italian and Portuguese bakeries and delis, and diners are never far away. Remember the full-service gas rule in New Jersey.

After a weekend in the Adirondack foothills, with their lakes and forests and long, empty roads, or a dawn ride through Bear Mountain and Harriman State Park, rolling into North Arlington is a sharp return to the dense, busy world of the New York suburbs. But the view from the ridge, with the skyline glittering across the marshes in the evening, is a good reminder of how close the wild hills are to the city, and how far you have come in a day.
t.old greenwich@41.0,-73.6:
Greenwich Point juts out into Long Island Sound at the edge of Old Greenwich, Connecticut, and the view from its shore is the reason to stop: a wide expanse of water dotted with sailboats, small rocky islands, and on a clear day the low line of Long Island on the horizon and, far to the southwest, the towers of Manhattan rising faintly from the haze. Old Greenwich itself is a pretty village of shingled houses, small shops and a little railway station, part of the wealthy town of Greenwich.

Greenwich Point Park, known locally as Tod's Point, was once a private estate, and the town bought it in the 1940s. It now has beaches, walking paths, salt marshes and an old stone building from the estate, and it is a favourite place for joggers, birdwatchers and families. In summer, access is limited to residents and their guests, with passes required, so for visitors the off-season, roughly autumn to spring, is the best time to visit. Outside summer, the park is quiet, and the light on the water early or late in the day is beautiful.

The riding to Old Greenwich is short and civilised. Shore Road and Sound Beach Avenue wind through the village and along the water, with big houses, stone walls and old trees. The Boston Post Road, US 1, runs through town with shops, restaurants and traffic lights. To the north, the Merritt Parkway, a historic road from the 1930s with ornate stone bridges and wooded borders, is a parkway built as much for looking as for driving, though trucks are banned and the lanes are narrow.

Old Greenwich has cafes, delis and a few restaurants, and fuel is easy to find on US 1. Greenwich, with its fancy shops and restaurants, is just a few minutes away.

For photographers, the best images here come in the golden hour, with the sun low over the water, or on a winter morning when the Sound is calm and grey and the islands seem to float. It is a gentle stop before the longer run north toward the Adirondack foothills and the wilder roads beyond.
t.near queenstown@-45.1,168.7:
South of Queenstown, the land runs along the eastern shore of Lake Wakatipu, between the water and the jagged wall of the Remarkables, and the road towards Kingston follows the lake for long kilometres. It is one of the most spectacular roads in New Zealand, with the lake on one side, deep blue and long, and the mountains rising steeply on the other, their peaks snow-capped for much of the year.

The Remarkables are the defining sight. They are a range of steep, jagged peaks, their name chosen because they look so remarkable, and their western face rises almost straight from the lake. In winter, a ski field operates on their upper slopes, reached by a steep gravel road. Lake Wakatipu itself is long and narrow, shaped like a lightning bolt, and it is said to "breathe": the water rises and falls by several centimetres every few minutes, a seiche caused by wind and pressure. Maori legend tells that the lake was formed when a giant, Matau, was burned in his sleep, and that his heart still beats beneath the water.

The ride to Queenstown from Wanaka over the Crown Range is the highlight of the day. The Crown Range Road is the highest main sealed road in New Zealand, with a summit at 1,076 metres, and it climbs in tight hairpins above the Cardrona valley, with huge views across the Wakatipu basin from the top. It can be closed or icy in winter, and the hairpins on the Queenstown side are steep, so ride carefully. Traffic includes campervans driven by tourists who may not be used to the roads, so give them room.

Queenstown is a busy resort town, known for adventure sports, bungee jumping and skiing, and it has every service you could need: fuel, food, accommodation and bike shops. To the south, Kingston is a small lakeside village at the end of the lake, where a historic steam train, the Kingston Flyer, has run at times. The roads to the south continue towards Fiordland and Southland.

Stop at a lakeside pullout, take off your helmet and watch the light change on the Remarkables in the late afternoon. It is one of those views that make you understand why people move to the other side of the world.
t.near bayonne@40.7,-74.2:
On the New Jersey side of New York Harbor, the Bayonne peninsula sticks out like a thumb between Newark Bay and Upper New York Bay, with the Statue of Liberty and the Manhattan skyline in view to the north-east. It is a working city of around sixty-five thousand people, built on oil refineries, shipyards and the port, and it still feels like a place where things are made and moved.

The views here are the reward for the urban riding. From the waterfront parks, you can see the towers of Lower Manhattan, the Statue of Liberty and the giant container ships moving through the harbour. At Harbor View Park, a huge bronze sculpture, the Teardrop memorial, designed by the Georgian artist Zurab Tsereteli, commemorates the victims of the September 11 attacks; it was a gift from Russia. The Bayonne Bridge, a great steel arch crossing the Kill van Kull to Staten Island, had its roadway raised in the 2010s to let bigger ships pass beneath it, an extraordinary piece of engineering.

The finish of a Litchfield Hills ride comes after a long day. The Litchfield Hills in north-west Connecticut are a land of rolling hills, small towns with white churches, lakes and forests, with winding roads through covered bridges and farms, and the ride there and back is full of good curves. Coming back, though, you must deal with the highways of New York and New Jersey, with heavy traffic, tolls and potholes. The New Jersey Turnpike, the Garden State Parkway and the bridges and tunnels around New York are notorious for congestion, and the last stretch can be slow and tiring.

Bayonne has fuel, food and services, and the surrounding area has every kind of restaurant. Port Newark and Elizabeth, across the bay, form one of the largest container ports in the country, and the sight of cranes and ships at sunset is striking in its own way.

Ride to the waterfront, kill the engine and watch the lights of Manhattan come on across the water. It is a fitting end to a ride from the quiet hills of Connecticut back into the heart of the metropolis.
t.levittown on the way back@40.7,-73.5:
Levittown is one of the most famous suburbs in the world, though it does not look like much at first glance. After the Second World War, the building firm Levitt and Sons bought potato fields on Long Island and built thousands of identical small houses on an assembly line, sold cheaply to returning soldiers and their families. It became the model for postwar suburbs across America, with its lawns, curving streets and shopping centres, and it also became a symbol of their darker side: for years the houses were sold only to white families, under covenants written into the deeds.

Today the houses have been extended, rebuilt and personalised beyond recognition, and the community has more than fifty thousand people. It is an ordinary suburb, with schools, shops and parks, and as a place to stop on the way back from the North Fork, it is practical rather than beautiful.

The swimming is a short ride south, at Jones Beach State Park, one of the great public beaches of the world. It was created in the 1920s by Robert Moses, the powerful planner who shaped much of New York's roads and parks, and it has miles of white sand facing the Atlantic, with lifeguards, boardwalks and an Art Deco water tower that stands over the beach like a lighthouse. The ocean is cold until July and the waves can be strong, so swim only between the flags, but on a hot summer day it is wonderful.

The North Fork of Long Island, where the ride goes, is very different from the busy western part of the island. It is a land of vineyards, farm stands, small towns and lighthouses, with quiet roads and views over Long Island Sound and Peconic Bay. The ride there and back uses the Long Island Expressway or the parkways, which can be slow with traffic, especially on summer weekends. Motorcycles are allowed on the parkways, which are often more pleasant than the expressway.

Levittown has fuel, food and every service, and the surrounding area has plenty of diners and delis. Grab a bagel or a sandwich, ride down to Jones Beach and cool off in the Atlantic before heading home.
t.bath beach@40.6,-74.0:
Bath Beach is a small neighbourhood on the south-west shore of Brooklyn, facing Gravesend Bay, and it got its name in the nineteenth century, when it was a seaside resort for wealthy New Yorkers, modelled on the English spa town of Bath. The resort is long gone, but the bay is still there, with a promenade along the water and views of the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, its great towers soaring over the entrance to New York Harbor.

The neighbourhood is part of the old Italian-American heart of Brooklyn, along with Bensonhurst next door, and you can still find old bakeries, pizzerias and social clubs, though today the area is also home to large Chinese and Russian communities. Eighty-sixth Street, under the elevated subway, is a busy shopping street with food from every corner of the world. A slice of pizza, a cannoli or a bowl of dumplings, all within a few blocks, make a good end to a ride.

The finish of a Bear Mountain and Harriman ride comes after a day in the hills of the Hudson Valley. Coming back, you use the Palisades Interstate Parkway or the New York Thruway, and then the bridges and expressways into Brooklyn, which can be slow and expensive with tolls.

Ride to the waterfront at the end of the day, watch the lights come on along the Verrazzano Bridge and listen to the waves of the bay. It is a peaceful moment after the noise and traffic of the city.
t.near boonton on the way back@41.0,-74.4:
The New Jersey Highlands are the surprise of the state for anyone who only knows it from the Turnpike. North-west of Boonton the land buckles into long wooded ridges of old granite and gneiss, with lakes in every hollow, rocky streams and roads that wriggle through forest for kilometre after kilometre. Boonton, Kinnelon and Butler sit on the edge of this country, small towns of seven to ten thousand people each, and they make a natural pause on the road back from Bear Mountain.

Boonton was an iron town. In the nineteenth century the falls of the Rockaway River powered a big ironworks here, fed by ore from the Highlands mines and by the Morris Canal, which climbed over the hills on inclined planes to carry coal and iron across the state. The ironworks have gone, but the gorge below the main street, now Grace Lord Park, still has the falls and a few old stone walls. On Pyramid Mountain, just outside Kinnelon, a glacial erratic called Tripod Rock, a boulder the size of a car balanced on three small stones, is a short hike from the road and one of the odder sights in the state.

Now the honest bit about swimming. Many of the lakes up here are reservoirs, like the big Boonton Reservoir, which supplies Jersey City and is strictly off limits, and many others are ringed by private lake communities with members-only beaches. For a public swim, head west to Lake Hopatcong, the largest lake in New Jersey, where Hopatcong State Park has a guarded beach in summer. It is a short ride, and the lake, busy with boats on weekends, has a cheerful old-resort feel.

The riding is quietly excellent. Route 23 is the main artery, fast and busy, but the side roads through Kinnelon, West Milford and the Wanaque area climb and twist along ridges, past reservoirs and through deep woods, with tight bends and blind crests. Surfaces vary from smooth to badly patched after winter frost, and deer are everywhere at dawn and dusk. Autumn, when the maples and oaks turn, is spectacular, and the traffic thins out after Labor Day.

Boonton has a pleasant old main street with cafés, diners and shops, and fuel is easy to find along Route 23 and the main roads. From here the last stretch back towards New York is quick on Interstate 287 and 80, so take a break, eat something and enjoy the trees before the traffic begins.
t.near easton on the way back@41.3,-73.2:
This corner of Fairfield County is horse fences, old stone walls, apple orchards and white clapboard houses set back among maples, the gentle face of Connecticut between the crowded shoreline and the hills to the north. Easton, with fewer than eight thousand people, has no real town centre at all, just farms, woods and winding roads, and much of its land is held as watershed for the reservoirs that supply Bridgeport and the coast.

It has had some remarkable residents. Helen Keller spent the last decades of her life at her home, Arcan Ridge, in Easton, and died there in 1968. Next door in Redding, Mark Twain built his last house, Stormfield, in 1908, and lived there until his death two years later. The countryside has not changed as much as you might expect since then: you can still ride past old farmhouses, red barns and fields where cows graze, and in autumn the farm stands sell apples, cider and pumpkins.

The nearest good options are a short ride either way: south to the beaches on Long Island Sound, such as Sherwood Island State Park in Westport, or north to Kettletown State Park on Lake Zoar, near Southbury, which has a swimming area in summer. The Sound is calm and fairly warm by late July; the lake is fresher and quieter.

The roads are a pleasure. Narrow, winding lanes run through the woods and around the reservoirs, with plenty of curves, short climbs and dips, and stone walls close to the road. Traffic is light outside rush hours, but watch for deer, cyclists and horse riders, and for police, who enforce the speed limits strictly. Coming back from the Delaware Water Gap, you will have spent most of the day on the busy Interstate 84; these back roads are a good way to finish more gently.

Trumbull, about twelve kilometres away, has fuel, shopping and services, and Newtown and the main roads have stations and diners too. Easton itself has a couple of general stores and farm stands. Stop for a cider donut, lean against a stone wall and take in the quiet before you head back to the city.
t.near east elmhurst@40.8,-73.9:
The planes give it away. East Elmhurst sits right beside LaGuardia Airport in northern Queens, and jets come in low over the rooftops every couple of minutes, their wheels down, as they line up for the runways that jut out into Flushing Bay. It is a neighbourhood of brick row houses, small gardens and churches, historically one of the main centres of Black middle-class life in Queens, and it has a strong sense of community despite the noise.

History is close at hand. Malcolm X lived here with his family in the early 1960s, and his house was firebombed in February 1965, a week before he was assassinated in Manhattan. Getting here means crossing into Queens on one of the big bridges, such as the Whitestone, the Throgs Neck or the Robert F. Kennedy Bridge, all with tolls, and then threading through dense traffic on the Grand Central Parkway or the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway. Fuel, food and services are everywhere, and the subway lines on Roosevelt Avenue will take you anywhere in the city. Flushing Meadows Corona Park, a short ride east, with the giant steel Unisphere from the 1964 World's Fair and the tennis stadiums of the US Open, is a good place to sit and watch the planes go by.
t.near blauvelt on the way back@41.1,-74.0:
Rockland County is the bit of New York State that feels like New Jersey and the Hudson Valley at the same time: suburban towns like Nanuet, West Nyack and Blauvelt, with shopping centres and highways, and then suddenly steep wooded ridges, cliffs above the river and old villages with church spires. Rockland Lake, a few kilometres north, was once the centre of a huge ice industry, where blocks of ice were cut in winter and shipped down the Hudson to New York City; today it is a state park with a lake for walking and boating, and swimming pools for summer. Tallman Mountain State Park, near Sparkill, also has a public pool. The lakes and reservoirs in the area, like Lake DeForest, are mostly off limits to swimmers.

t.near lyndhurst@40.8,-74.1:
The Meadowlands are one of the strangest landscapes in America: a vast flat expanse of marsh and reeds along the Hackensack River, criss-crossed by highways, railways and power lines, with the Manhattan skyline rising across the water to the east. t.near bayonne@40.7,-74.1:
The Kill van Kull is a narrow tidal strait between Bayonne in New Jersey and the North Shore of Staten Island, and it is one of the busiest waterways in the country. Enormous container ships, tankers and tugs squeeze through it on their way to and from the port at Newark and Elizabeth, passing so close to the shore that you feel you could touch them. t.east norwalk@41.1,-73.4:
Nobody will pretend there is a mountain pass in East Norwalk. t.ocean grove@40.2,-74.0:
Ocean Grove is one of the oddest and most charming towns on the Jersey Shore. Around it, in summer, stand the canvas tents of the camp meeting, small wooden cabins with canvas fronts that families have rented for generations.

For a long time the town was dry and strictly observed the Sabbath: until the late twentieth century, cars were not allowed on the streets on Sundays, and the beach was closed on Sunday mornings. The rules have relaxed, but Ocean Grove still has a calmer, more family-oriented atmosphere than many shore towns. Once you leave it, the local roads are slow and congested in season, with traffic lights and pedestrians everywhere. t.near fort hamilton@40.6,-74.0:
The Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge leaps across the entrance to New York Harbor between Brooklyn and Staten Island, and this ride's start and finish sit at its foot, near Fort Hamilton on the Brooklyn side and Fort Wadsworth across the water. Every November the New York City Marathon begins on it.

Between them, ships of every kind pass in and out of the harbour, from container ships to cruise liners. Along the Brooklyn shore, the Shore Road promenade offers views of the bridge and the harbour, and it is a pleasant place to walk.

New York traffic is heavy and aggressive, and the roads are often in poor condition, with potholes and construction.

Bay Ridge, the neighbourhood around Fort Hamilton, has plenty of fuel stations, diners, pizza places and restaurants. Leave early in the morning, especially on summer weekends, to avoid the worst of the traffic, and allow plenty of time for the return.
t.emerson hill@40.6,-74.1:
Most visitors to New York never see Staten Island except from the deck of the free ferry, which is a pity, because its interior holds something unexpected: a ridge of steep, wooded hills running through the middle of the island. The local streets on Emerson Hill are steep and narrow, with tight bends. t.dover beaches north@40.0,-74.1:
When Hurricane Sandy struck the Jersey Shore in October 2012, Ortley Beach, part of Dover Beaches North, was one of the hardest-hit places on the coast. The storm surge swept across the barrier island, destroying hundreds of houses and leaving sand piled in the streets. The community has been rebuilt, with new houses raised on stilts, but the memory of the storm is still fresh.

Route 35 runs along the island, through a string of beach towns, and the ocean beaches are wide and sandy, with lifeguards in summer. Seaside Heights, to the south, has a boardwalk with amusement rides, arcades and food stands.

Barnegat Bay, on the western side of the island, is shallow and calm, popular with boaters, kayakers and crabbers. Blue crabs are a local delicacy, and the seafood shacks along the bay serve them steamed, with Old Bay seasoning.
