t.branford center@41.3,-72.8:
The base of the Statue of Liberty is made of pink granite from Stony Creek, a village in Branford, and the quarries on the shore still cut stone today. Off the coast, the Thimble Islands, a scattering of more than a hundred small granite islands, some with a single house perched on the rock, dot the water of Long Island Sound. Boat tours from Stony Creek wind among them in summer, telling tales of pirates, millionaires and General Tom Thumb, the famous circus showman, who is said to have courted a woman on one of the islands.

The riding on the Connecticut shore is pleasant, with Route 1 and the shore roads winding through the towns and along the water. I-95 is fast but often congested. The roads inland are quieter, with woods, stone walls and farms.

Fuel is easiest along Route 1. The Connecticut lobster roll is served hot with butter, not cold with mayonnaise as in Maine, and locals will happily argue that theirs is the only correct version. Order one at a shack near the water and decide for yourself.
t.milford@41.2,-73.1:
Captain Kidd, the pirate, is said to have buried treasure on Charles Island, off the coast of Milford, in 1699, shortly before his arrest and execution. Nobody has found it, but the legend lives on. The island is connected to the mainland at low tide by a sandbar, and you can walk across from Silver Sands State Park. Be careful: the tide comes in fast, and people get stranded every year.

Milford is one of the oldest towns in Connecticut, founded in 1639 by Puritan settlers, and its centre has a long green, old churches and houses, and a harbour where oyster boats once worked. The Wepawaug river runs through the town, with a duck pond and a waterfall near the green.

The beaches along the Milford shore are sandy and calm, with views across Long Island Sound. Silver Sands State Park has a boardwalk through the dunes and salt marsh, with birds and wildflowers.

This stop marks the end of the ride from the Taconic hills, a day of backroads through the woods and farms of the Hudson Valley, and the coast is a pleasant contrast. The final stretch follows the Merritt Parkway or I-95, both often congested.

Fuel is everywhere on the Boston Post Road. Down at the harbour, where the oyster fleet once worked, fried clams with a cold drink and the Sound turning silver at dusk make a fitting full stop to a day of Hudson Valley back roads.
t.ridgefield@40.8,-74.0:
Before Hollywood, there was Fort Lee. In the early 1900s the cliffs and towns along this stretch of the Hudson were the centre of American film-making, with studios turning out westerns, serials and melodramas, and serial heroines were filmed dangling from the very cliffs you ride above. The industry moved west for the sunshine, but the story is a good one to carry into the last miles of a ride.

Ridgefield is a small Bergen County borough just west of Fort Lee and the George Washington Bridge, sitting between the ridge of the Palisades and the marshes of the Hackensack Meadowlands. It is dense, busy suburbia, with Korean, Italian and Greek groceries side by side, and the restaurants along Broad Avenue in neighbouring Palisades Park make this one of the best places on the East Coast for Korean food.

History runs deeper too. In November 1776 Washington's army abandoned Fort Lee as the British crossed the Hudson, beginning the long retreat across New Jersey that ended with the surprise victory at Trenton. A reconstructed camp in Fort Lee Historic Park sits on the cliff edge, with views straight across to Manhattan.

Coming back from the Croton reservoirs and the river towns, the Palisades Interstate Parkway is the best way in, a wooded, curving road along the top of the cliffs with lookouts over the Hudson. The final stretch into Ridgefield is all junctions, lights and the approach roads to the bridge, which can lock solid at rush hour.

Fuel in New Jersey is still pumped for you by an attendant by law, which surprises visitors; just stay on the bike, say regular, and let them work. Then go and find a Korean barbecue table in Palisades Park.
t.port richmond@40.6,-74.1:
Staten Island's north shore faces New Jersey across the narrow Kill Van Kull, and Port Richmond sits right on it, under the steel arch of the Bayonne Bridge. That bridge was raised in recent years, its roadway lifted higher on the old arch so that the giant container ships heading for Newark and Elizabeth could pass underneath, an engineering feat carried out while traffic still flowed. From the waterfront, you watch tugs and ships slide past almost close enough to touch.

Port Richmond was once a busy commercial centre, with shipyards, oyster beds and a main street of shops and theatres. It declined in the twentieth century and has been revived in recent decades by Mexican and Latin American immigrants, whose bakeries, taquerias and grocery stores now line the old streets. The neighbourhood also has an old pizzeria that New Yorkers cross boroughs for, and tavern-style thin-crust pizza is something of a Staten Island tradition.

The Staten Island Ferry, free and running around the clock from St George, a few kilometres east, gives one of the best views of the Statue of Liberty and the Manhattan skyline. It does not take vehicles anymore, but it is worth a round trip on foot.

Coming back from the Delaware Water Gap, the final stretch crosses New Jersey on the interstates and arrives over the Goethals or Bayonne bridges, both tolled. Traffic is heavy at rush hour, and the roads on Staten Island are often congested.

Fuel and food are easy on Richmond Avenue and Forest Avenue. Before you go home, find a spot on the waterfront near the bridge at dusk: a ship the size of a city block easing under the arch, its lights coming on, is a strange and wonderful last image after a day on Pennsylvania's river roads.
t.harrison@40.7,-74.2:
The New York Red Bulls play football at a sleek stadium on the banks of the Passaic river in Harrison, and on match days the small town fills with fans. Harrison is an old industrial town in Hudson County, New Jersey, across the river from Newark, where factories once made thread, steel and light bulbs. Many of the old works have been demolished and replaced with apartment towers, and the PATH train connects the town to Manhattan.

Across the river, the Ironbound district of Newark is famous for its Portuguese, Brazilian and Spanish restaurants, serving grilled meats, seafood and wine. The neighbourhood got its name from the railway lines that surrounded it, and it is one of the most vibrant food scenes in the New York area.

There is no great scenery to reward you at the end, but there is food. Cross the bridge into the Ironbound, find a rodízio where waiters keep bringing skewers of grilled meat until you surrender, and wash it down with a glass of vinho verde. Fuel is on every main road, attendant service included, as everywhere in New Jersey.

On match nights, check the fixtures before you plan your route. The streets around the stadium close and fill with fans, and parking a bike becomes a negotiation.
t.sayreville on the way back@40.5,-74.4:
Sayreville was built on clay. For more than a century the pits along the Raritan river supplied brick works that sent millions of bricks up the river and across the bay to build New York, and the town's lakes and ponds are mostly old clay pits filled with water. Later it became a gunpowder and chemical town, and later still the hometown of Jon Bon Jovi, which is the fact most visitors already know.

The town sits on the south bank of the Raritan, near where the river widens into Raritan Bay, and the Garden State Parkway crosses the water on the Driscoll Bridge, a structure with so many lanes that it has been described as one of the widest bridges in the world. t.near east rutherford@40.8,-74.1:
The Hackensack Meadowlands were once written off as a wasteland of marsh, dumps and smouldering garbage, the place where gangsters supposedly disposed of their problems. Today they are something unexpected: a recovering wetland, full of herons, egrets and ospreys, wrapped around a stadium that holds more than eighty thousand people. This finish lies at the edge of that landscape, near East Rutherford, Carlstadt and Moonachie.

MetLife Stadium, home of both the New York Giants and the New York Jets, rises above the reeds, and next to it the American Dream mall, a vast complex with an indoor ski slope and water park, adds a surreal touch. On game days, traffic in the area is terrible, so check the schedule.

The Meadowlands also has some real nature. Parks along the Hackensack river have boardwalks through the marshes, and the restored wetlands are a haven for birds, a remarkable recovery from decades of pollution. Teterboro airport, nearby, is the busiest private jet airport in the New York area.

Coming back from the Poconos, the final stretch follows I-80 or Route 3, both often congested, and the roads around the Meadowlands are a maze of ramps and junctions. Watch for potholes, trucks and drivers who change lanes without warning.

East Rutherford and Carlstadt are small, low-rise boroughs with diners, delis and Italian bakeries. Fuel is everywhere, pumped by an attendant as New Jersey law requires. If you finish at sunset, look west over the marsh, with the stadium behind you; the light on the reeds can be surprisingly beautiful.
t.belmar@40.2,-74.0:
In January 1946, at Camp Evans, an army research base a few kilometres inland from Belmar, engineers bounced a radar signal off the Moon and detected the echo for the first time. Project Diana, as it was called, marked the birth of radar astronomy and the space age, and the site is now home to a museum of communications history.

Belmar is a classic Jersey Shore beach town, with a wide sandy beach, a boardwalk and streets of wooden houses. The Shark River inlet, at the northern end of town, is busy with fishing boats and pleasure craft, and the marina is a good place to watch the boats come and go. In summer, the town is packed with young people, and the bars are loud.

This stop marks the start of a ride into the Jersey Highlands, a region of wooded ridges, lakes and twisting roads in the north of the state. Leaving early, before the traffic builds, is the best way to start the day.

For food, Belmar has diners, bakeries and seafood restaurants, and the boardwalk stands sell coffee, egg sandwiches and pork roll, a New Jersey breakfast meat that locals call Taylor ham in the north. The debate over the name is fierce, and visitors are advised not to take sides.

If you have time for a quick swim before setting off, the beach is wide and guarded in summer, though like most Jersey Shore towns Belmar charges a beach fee in season. Fuel is on Route 35 and Route 71, where an attendant will fill the tank while you finish your coffee.
Gliders have been launching from the airfield at Wurtsboro since the late 1920s, and it claims to be the oldest soaring site in the United States. On summer afternoons, sailplanes circle silently over the Shawangunk Ridge, riding the thermals and the updrafts along the cliffs. The spot is close to Wurtsboro, in the valley between the Shawangunks and the Catskills, in Sullivan County, New York.

The Delaware and Hudson Canal, which carried coal from Pennsylvania to the Hudson in the nineteenth century, ran through this valley, and traces of the old towpath and locks survive. The Bashakill, a large marsh south of Wurtsboro, is a wildlife area full of birds, beavers and turtles, with trails and a boardwalk.

Sullivan County was the heart of the Borscht Belt, the resort area where Jewish families from New York spent their summers in the mid-twentieth century, and comedians like Jerry Lewis and Joan Rivers started their careers in the hotel showrooms. Most of the big hotels have closed, but the memory lingers.

For a swim, the lakes of Sullivan County have beaches and swimming areas, and some state parks have designated areas. Check before you go, as rules vary.

The roads are the reason to linger. Route 209 runs along the valley with the ridge always in view, and the climb over the Shawangunks on Route 52 towards Ellenville gives a famous lookout over the whole valley to the Catskills. Surfaces vary, frost heaves are common, and deer are everywhere at dusk. Wurtsboro's small main street has fuel and a diner or two, and Ellenville has more.
t.near port jervis on the way back@41.3,-7:
Three states meet in the middle of the Delaware river at Port Jervis, where the Neversink flows in from the north, and a stone marker on a spit of land at the confluence lets you stand almost in New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania at once. This stop lies just south of there, near Milford, Pennsylvania, at the northern end of the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area, where the river runs wide and clear between forested ridges.

Milford is a handsome small town with a grand stone mansion on the hill above it. Grey Towers was the home of Gifford Pinchot, the first chief of the United States Forest Service and the man who more or less invented American forest conservation, and it is open to visitors. The town's streets are lined with old inns, galleries and cafés.

North of Port Jervis, Route 97 climbs onto the cliffs above the Delaware at Hawk's Nest, a stretch of road carved into the rock with stone walls and sweeping views down to the river, which carmakers have used in countless adverts. It is short but spectacular, and on summer weekends it is crowded with bikes.

The Delaware is clean, cool and inviting in summer, and people tube, canoe and swim in it in great numbers. But the river is also dangerous: its currents are strong and its depth changes suddenly, and drownings occur every year. The park service urges everyone to wear a life jacket on the water, and you should swim only at designated beaches with lifeguards.

Route 209, which runs south through the recreation area, is a pleasant, wooded road along the river, with waterfalls a short walk from the road at Dingmans Ferry and Raymondskill. Speed limits are low and enforced. Milford and Port Jervis have fuel, diners and shops.
t.near woodstock@44.0,-71.7:
The Kancamagus Highway crosses the White Mountains of New Hampshire for some fifty-five kilometres between Lincoln and Conway, and for all that distance there is not a single gas station, restaurant or shop. That is what makes it special: one of the most beautiful roads in New England, through unbroken forest, along rivers and over a mountain pass, with nothing commercial to interrupt it. This stop lies near its western end, close to Lincoln and North Woodstock, where the road leaves the valley and begins to climb.

The highway is named after Kancamagus, a seventeenth-century sachem of the Pennacook people, who tried to keep peace with the English settlers before being driven north. The road was completed in the late 1950s and paved through in the 1960s, and it has been protected from development ever since.

In late September and early October, when the maples, birches and beeches turn red, orange and gold, the Kancamagus becomes one of the most famous foliage drives in America, and the traffic can be bumper to bumper on weekends. At other times of year it is quiet, with moose in the wetlands at dawn and dusk.

The Swift River runs alongside the eastern half of the road, and at the Lower Falls, a series of granite ledges and pools, people swim and sunbathe on hot summer days. Sabbaday Falls, a short walk from the road, is a narrow gorge with a waterfall. Parking at the trailheads requires a recreation pass, available from self-service stations.

The riding is a joy, with long, flowing bends, a steady climb to the pass and a winding descent. The surface is good, but frost heaves can be sharp in spring. Fill up in Lincoln before you start, and carry food and water.
t.near cromwell@-45.1,169.1:
Cromwell sits where two of Central Otago's big rivers used to meet, and these days the meeting happens under water. When the Clyde Dam was finished in the early 1990s, the rising Lake Dunstan swallowed the old town centre and much of the gorge, and what survived of the gold-era main street was rebuilt as a heritage precinct on the new lakeshore. It is worth the short detour: schist cottages, a bakery or two, and the eerie knowledge that the original riverbank is somewhere below the boats.

The riding around here is a matter of light and space. State Highway 6 runs west through the Kawarau Gorge towards Queenstown, a tight, rocky slot with the milky river far below and bungy jumpers dropping off the old bridge at the far end. North, State Highway 8 heads up past Tarras towards the Lindis Pass, all long tawny hills and wide bends that let you see oncoming traffic a kilometre away. South towards Clyde and Alexandra the road follows the lake through bare schist country that looks almost lunar in the late afternoon.

This is the driest corner of New Zealand, and the summer heat is real; in winter, frost can glaze the shady bends well into the morning, so do not trust the gorge before the sun has been on it. Wind funnels down the lake too, which you will feel on an exposed motorcycle crossing the bridges.

The gold rush of the 1860s first brought people here, but the money now is in stone fruit and wine. Bannockburn, just across the water, grows some of the most southerly Pinot Noir in the world, and roadside stalls sell cherries and apricots in midsummer. Cromwell itself is a proper service town with several fuel stations, supermarkets and cafés, so it is the natural place to fill the tank and eat before the longer, emptier stretches toward Haast, Te Anau or the Lindis, where the next pump can be a long way off.
t.near dayton@40.4,-74.5:
Central New Jersey is not where anyone goes looking for mountain roads, and Dayton, part of South Brunswick township, makes no pretence otherwise. It sits in the flat country between New Brunswick and Princeton, crossed by Route 130, the New Jersey Turnpike and US 1, with warehouses, office parks, farms that have survived development and a lot of commuters. Think of this as a place to regroup on the way to the good stuff rather than a destination in itself.

That said, a little local knowledge makes the area surprisingly pleasant. Head west towards Kingston and Princeton and you meet the Delaware and Raritan Canal, dug in the 1830s to move coal between Philadelphia and New York, now a long, tree-shaded park with a towpath and old lock-tender houses. The back roads around it are flat but leafy, especially in autumn. Princeton itself has the university, a famous Revolutionary War battlefield from January 1777, and plenty of cafés along Nassau Street.

From here the routes that make the trip worthwhile point north-west, towards the Sourland Mountain ridge and eventually the Delaware Water Gap, or north towards the Hudson Highlands. Expect traffic signals, aggressive commuter driving at peak hours and some rough patched asphalt; summer brings heat and humidity that make an early start very sensible.

The practical side is easy. Fuel stations are everywhere along the main highways, and New Jersey still does not allow drivers to pump their own fuel, so you wait for an attendant, which is either charming or maddening depending on your mood. Diners, delis and chain coffee shops are never far away. Take the break here, check the route, and save your energy for the hills further on.
t.parsippany@40.9,-74.4:
Parsippany-Troy Hills is suburban New Jersey at its most typical: office parks, shopping centres and the enormous junction of Interstate 80 and Interstate 287, one of the busiest crossroads in the state. Nobody comes here for the scenery, but it is a useful launch point, because the good roads of northern New Jersey begin just beyond the town limits.

The area has a surprising amount of water. Lake Parsippany and the Boonton and Jersey City reservoirs lie close by, and Troy Meadows, one of the largest freshwater wetlands in the state, is home to herons and turtles despite the highways around it. Ride north-west and the ground rises into the New Jersey Highlands, a band of ancient gneiss ridges that runs towards the Hudson. That is where the roads start to twist: tree-lined two-lane routes past lakes and old iron-mining villages, with the Wanaque and Splitrock reservoirs as calm stops.

The local riding is all about avoiding rush hour. Weekday mornings and evenings clog Route 46, Route 10 and the interstates, while early weekend mornings can be wonderfully empty. Expect potholes after harsh winters, plenty of traffic lights and the occasional deer bounding out of the woods on the smaller roads, especially at dusk in autumn.

Fuel is everywhere, and as anywhere in New Jersey, an attendant pumps it for you. Diners are a local institution, many open very long hours, and this part of the state has plenty of them, along with bagel shops and delis for a quick breakfast before heading out. If you are heading for the Hudson Valley or the Delaware Water Gap, this is a good point to check the bike, fill the tank and drink one last coffee before the scenery improves.
t.near fort salonga@40.9,-73.3:
Fort Salonga takes its name from a British stronghold of the Revolutionary War. Fort Slongo stood on a bluff above Long Island Sound, and in 1781 American troops crossed the water from Connecticut and raided it. Nothing much remains, but the name lives on in this leafy corner of the North Shore, between Kings Park and Northport, where wooded hills drop to rocky beaches and the Sound glitters to the north.

Riding here means Route 25A, the old North Shore road that wanders east from the city through villages, past estates and over gentle hills. It is not fast, but it is pretty, with stone walls, old churches and the occasional glimpse of the water. Nearby, Sunken Meadow State Park has a long boardwalk and views across to the Connecticut shore, and the bluffs at Fort Salonga itself offer a quiet stop with similar outlooks.

Traffic can be heavy, especially on summer weekends when half of Long Island heads to the beaches, and the road is lined with driveways and junctions, so stay alert. Deer are common at dusk. Northport, just to the east, is a lovely harbour village with a main street sloping down to the water, cafés and a long maritime history, including shipbuilding and oystering.

For fuel and food, Northport, Kings Park and Commack all have plenty of choice, and delis and bagel shops abound. From here, the route continues east towards the North Fork, where the land narrows, vineyards and farm stands replace the suburbs, and the lighthouses at the end of the island beckon. Fort Salonga is a gentle pause on the way, a reminder that even the busy North Shore keeps pockets of history and quiet.
t.point lookout@40.6,-73.6:
Calling Point Lookout a high point is a joke the place itself would appreciate: it sits barely above sea level at the eastern tip of the Long Beach barrier island, where the Atlantic meets Jones Inlet. What it offers instead is a lookout in the literal sense, a wide view across the inlet to Jones Beach, with its famous water tower, and out over the ocean, where container ships wait their turn for New York Harbor.

The hamlet is a quiet community of beach houses, seafood restaurants and fishing boats, far more relaxed than the busy resort of Long Beach to the west. In 2012, Hurricane Sandy flooded much of the barrier island, and the scars of that storm, along with the rebuilt dunes and raised houses, are a reminder of the fragility of life on the edge of the sea. The beaches here are wide and sandy, and the marshes behind the island are full of birds.

The riding here is about the coast rather than curves. The Loop Parkway connects Point Lookout to Jones Beach across the inlet, and the Ocean Parkway runs east along the barrier islands towards Fire Island, a long, flat ride with the ocean on one side and the bay on the other. Wind is a constant factor, and sand can blow onto the road. Summer weekends bring heavy traffic to the beaches.

Point Lookout has a few restaurants and delis, but fuel is more easily found in Long Beach or Oceanside. A plate of clams or a lobster roll by the water is the classic choice. The Vermont mountains are a world away to the north, but the sea breeze here is a fine start.
t.nanuet@41.1,-74.0:
Nanuet is suburban Rockland County through and through, a place of shopping centres, highway junctions and quiet residential streets just west of the Hudson. Nobody rides here for the scenery, but its location is excellent, because some of the best riding near New York City starts a few miles away.

To the north and west lie Harriman and Bear Mountain state parks, a huge expanse of forests, lakes and rocky ridges in the Hudson Highlands. The roads through them, such as Seven Lakes Drive and the Perkins Memorial Drive up Bear Mountain, are winding and scenic, with views over the Hudson and the surrounding hills. The Palisades Interstate Parkway runs north from the George Washington Bridge along the cliffs of the Palisades, a fast and beautiful route out of the city. The parks were created in the early twentieth century, partly to stop quarrying that was destroying the Palisades cliffs.

The riding in the parks is excellent, but the roads can be busy on summer weekends, with hikers, cyclists and families, and speed limits are strictly enforced. Deer are common, especially at dawn and dusk. In autumn, the foliage is spectacular, and the roads are at their best.

Nanuet has plenty of fuel stations, diners, delis and coffee shops, and unlike in New Jersey across the state line, you can pump your own fuel here. It is a good place to fill up and grab a coffee before heading into the parks or north towards the Catskills and Vermont. From the top of Bear Mountain, the view over the Hudson is one of the best in the region.
t.near little silver@40.3,-74.1:
Little Silver occupies a neck of land between two tidal rivers, the Navesink and the Shrewsbury, in the comfortable heart of Monmouth County. It is an old place by American standards, settled in the seventeenth century, and the river shores around it are lined with marinas, big houses and marshes where ospreys nest on platforms in summer. Red Bank, next door, is a lively small town with theatres and restaurants, and it was the birthplace of the jazz bandleader Count Basie, whose name is on the town's grand old theatre.

The riding is gentle and pleasant rather than exciting. Roads curve along the rivers, cross low bridges and pass through leafy towns, with water views at every turn. Heading east, Rumson Road runs past grand estates towards the ocean at Sea Bright, a narrow strip of sand between the Shrewsbury River and the Atlantic. To the north, the Highlands rise surprisingly steeply above the bay, and the Twin Lights, a castle-like pair of lighthouse towers, look out over Sandy Hook and the approaches to New York Harbor. On a clear day the Manhattan skyline is visible across the water.

Sandy Hook itself, a long barrier spit now part of a national recreation area, has beaches, an old army fort and the oldest working lighthouse in the United States, built in 1764. Summer weekends clog the roads to the shore, and parking at the beaches fills early. Wind off the ocean can be strong, and sea fog occasionally rolls in.

Fuel is easy to find in Red Bank and along Route 35, with attendants pumping as everywhere in New Jersey. Red Bank's main street has cafés, bakeries and restaurants, making it the natural place to stop and eat before turning inland.
t.near suffern@41.1,-74.2:
Suffern guards the Ramapo Pass, the narrow gap where the Ramapo River cuts through the Highlands at the New York and New Jersey border. During the Revolution, this gap was a vital route between the Hudson and the colonies to the south, and Continental troops were stationed here to keep it open; Washington himself passed through more than once. Today, the pass carries the New York Thruway, Route 17 and a railway, all squeezed into the valley, and Suffern is a busy small village at its mouth.

The Ramapo Mountains rise steeply on both sides, covered with oak and hickory forests, and they are part of the Highlands that stretch from Pennsylvania to Connecticut. Harriman State Park, just to the north, is a vast area of lakes, forests and rocky ridges, laced with hiking trails and winding roads. In autumn, the foliage is spectacular, with the hills ablaze with red, orange and gold.

The riding from Suffern is excellent. Route 17 north through the Ramapo valley is busy, but the roads into Harriman, such as Seven Lakes Drive, are a delight, winding past lakes and through forests. Heading west, roads lead towards Greenwood Lake and the Warwick valley, with more curves and fewer cars. Traffic can be heavy on weekends and around the outlet stores at Central Valley, and deer are a real hazard at dusk.

Suffern has fuel stations, delis, diners and coffee shops, and you can pump your own fuel on the New York side of the border. It is a good place to fill up and grab a bite before heading into the mountains, towards Montauk on the far end of Long Island or the high peaks of the Catskills.
t.mendham@40.8,-74.6:
The winter of 1779 to 1780 was one of the harshest on record, and the Continental Army spent it in huts at Jockey Hollow, a few miles east of Mendham, short of food, clothing and pay. Soldiers froze, starved and deserted, and some mutinied, yet the army survived. The site is now part of Morristown National Historical Park, with reconstructed huts, an old farmhouse and quiet woodland trails, and it is a moving place to stop.

Mendham itself is a small, well-kept colonial village in the hills of Morris County, with white churches, old taverns and a crossroads that has been a meeting point for centuries. The surrounding countryside is horse country, with rolling pastures, stone walls, big estates and wooded hills. It is one of the most attractive corners of northern New Jersey, and the roads through it are among the most pleasant in the region.

The riding here is a joy. Roads wind over hills and through valleys, past farms, forests and streams, with constant changes of direction and gradient. The surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel, potholes after winter and horse riders on the lanes. Traffic is moderate, but local drivers can be impatient, and police patrol regularly. In autumn, the leaves turn spectacular colours, and the roads are at their best.

Mendham has a deli, a few cafés and restaurants, and fuel is available nearby, although Morristown, a short ride east, has a wider choice of services. A coffee in the village, followed by a walk at Jockey Hollow, makes a satisfying break. Northwards, the Catskills promise high peaks and longer, wilder roads.
t.near shrewsbury@40.2,-74.5:
Inland from Shrewsbury and the Jersey Shore, western Monmouth County is a surprise to anyone who thinks New Jersey is all highways and suburbs. This is farm country, with horse paddocks, sod farms, orchards and fields of corn and soybeans, crossed by quiet roads and dotted with small villages. Allentown, a few miles west, is a delightful old mill town with a millpond, a main street of eighteenth-century houses and antique shops.

The area has deep historical roots. A short ride north-east, near Freehold, the Battle of Monmouth was fought on a scorching day in June 1778, one of the largest battles of the Revolution. Legend says that a woman known as Molly Pitcher carried water to the soldiers and took her husband's place at a cannon when he collapsed, and the battlefield is now a state park with a visitor centre and walking trails across the orchards and fields.

The riding here is gentle and pleasant, with roads winding between farms and through small woods. The land is flat to gently rolling, with few challenging bends, but the scenery is pleasant and the traffic light compared with the rest of the state. Watch for farm vehicles, horses and deer, and for sandy patches at the edges of the road. Summer brings heat and humidity, while autumn is crisp and colourful.

Fuel and food are available in Allentown, Freehold and the larger towns along the main roads, with attendants pumping fuel as everywhere in New Jersey. Farm stands sell fresh produce, pies and cider in season, and local diners offer hearty breakfasts. It is an easy place for a quiet halt before heading towards Long Island and its lighthouses.
t.near kiryas joel@41.4,-74.1:
The village of Kiryas Joel, in Orange County north-west of New York City, is one of the most distinctive communities in the United States, founded in the 1970s by Satmar Hasidic Jews and still almost entirely Hasidic today. It is a densely built, fast-growing village where Yiddish is widely spoken, shops close for the Sabbath and the rhythm of life follows religious tradition. Visitors passing through should be respectful and dress modestly if stopping.

The surrounding countryside is far less dense. To the south and east lie the forests and lakes of Harriman State Park and the Hudson Highlands, and to the north the long ridge of Schunemunk Mountain, a wild and rugged hill with views over the Hudson valley. To the west, beyond the Wallkill valley, rise the white cliffs of the Shawangunk Ridge, famous among rock climbers, with the lakes of Minnewaska State Park on top.

The riding around here is varied. Route 17 and the Thruway are busy, especially near the outlet shopping centre at Central Valley, but the minor roads into the hills are much more rewarding, winding through forests and farmland with views of the ridges. Traffic can be heavy on weekends and holidays, and deer are a constant hazard.

Fuel, delis and diners are plentiful in Monroe and the surrounding towns, and you can pump your own fuel in New York. Kosher food is widely available in the village itself. Fill up here before heading west towards the Shawangunks, where the roads climb onto the ridge and the views open out over the valleys.
t.old bethpage@40.8,-73.5:
Step into Old Bethpage Village Restoration and Long Island's suburbs vanish: a nineteenth-century farming village of houses, barns, a church, a tavern and a blacksmith's shop, many of them moved here from elsewhere on the island to save them from demolition. Costumed staff work the fields and crafts, and the contrast with the busy roads outside is striking.

The surrounding area is classic Nassau and Suffolk County suburbia, with houses, shopping centres and parkways. But it has its own claims to fame. Bethpage State Park, next door, is home to the Black Course, one of the toughest public golf courses in the United States, which has hosted the US Open. And in nearby Bethpage, the Grumman aircraft company built fighter planes for the Second World War and the Lunar Module that landed astronauts on the Moon, a remarkable piece of history for a suburban town.

The riding here is not particularly exciting, with traffic lights, busy roads and suburban sprawl. The Bethpage State Parkway and the Northern State Parkway offer faster routes through the area, with tree-lined curves, but traffic can be heavy. The roads towards the North Shore, with its hills and estates, are more interesting, and the Gold Coast mansions that inspired The Great Gatsby are not far away.

Old Bethpage has plenty of fuel stations, delis and diners, and the bagels are as good as anywhere on the island. It is a good place to stop for a break before heading east towards the North Fork, where farms, vineyards and lighthouses replace the suburbs and the island narrows to its tip.
t.near nyack@41.1,-73.9:
Edward Hopper, the painter of lonely diners and empty streets, was born in Nyack in 1882, and his childhood home is now a small art centre. The village has always attracted artists and writers, and it has a lively, slightly bohemian atmosphere, with antique shops, cafés and galleries on streets that slope down to the Hudson River.

Nyack sits on the west bank of the Hudson at its widest point, the Tappan Zee, where the river swells into a broad lake. The new Governor Mario M. Cuomo Bridge, which replaced the old Tappan Zee Bridge in 2017 and 2018, spans the river here, with a path for walkers and cyclists and views up and down the valley. To the north, the cliffs of Hook Mountain rise above the river, and the Palisades stretch south towards New York City.

The riding from Nyack is excellent. Route 9W heads north along the river, with views over the water and the hills, towards Haverstraw and Bear Mountain. The roads into the hills behind the village, towards the Hudson Highlands and Harriman State Park, are winding and scenic. Traffic can be heavy in the village and on the main roads, especially at weekends, and parking can be difficult. Cyclists are common on 9W, which is a popular training route.

Nyack has fuel stations, cafés, bakeries and restaurants, making it a pleasant place to stop. A coffee by the river, watching the boats and the bridge, is a fine way to break the ride. The Berkshires and the Mohawk Trail lie far to the north, a long but rewarding ride through the Hudson valley and the hills of New England.
t.near bloomingdale@40.5,-74.7:
The long, wooded ridge of Sourland Mountain rises out of the farmland of Somerset County here, a lump of hard volcanic rock that resisted erosion while the softer land around it was worn away. The Sourlands are not high, but they are wild for New Jersey, with boulder fields, streams and forests, and they make a welcome change from the flat suburbs further east. It was on this ridge that Charles Lindbergh built his house, and from which his baby son was kidnapped in 1932, a crime that gripped the nation.

The surrounding countryside of Hillsborough and Montgomery is a mix of farms, horse paddocks, old villages and newer housing. Nearby, Duke Farms, the former estate of the tobacco heiress Doris Duke, is now a nature preserve with meadows, lakes and woodland, open to visitors. The Raritan River and its tributaries wind through the area, lined with trees and old mill buildings.

From the saddle it is pleasant and varied. The roads over the Sourland ridge are narrow and winding, with steep sections and blind corners, while the roads through the farmland are gentler. Traffic is moderate, but local drivers can be fast, and deer are a constant hazard. Surfaces can be rough after winter, and gravel collects in the corners.

Fuel, delis and diners are available in Hillsborough, Somerville and along Route 206, with attendants pumping as everywhere in New Jersey. A farm stand or a small café makes a good break. From the ridge, the views over the farmland are rewarding, especially in autumn, when the colours are at their best.
t.near hackettstown@40.9,-74.9:
Hackettstown smells faintly of chocolate on some days, thanks to the Mars factory in town, where candy has been made for decades. It is a pleasant small town in the valley of the Musconetcong River, in the hills of north-western New Jersey, with a main street, old churches and a college. For riders, it is a gateway to some of the best roads in the state.

The Musconetcong is a lovely river, flowing south-west towards the Delaware through a valley of farms, forests and old mill villages. It has been designated a National Wild and Scenic River, and its banks are lined with trees and meadows. To the north and west, the land rises into the Kittatinny Ridge and the Delaware Water Gap, where the Delaware River cuts through the ridge in a dramatic gorge.

The riding from Hackettstown is excellent. Route 57 and the roads along the Musconetcong are scenic and winding, while the roads over Schooley's Mountain and towards the Water Gap offer steeper climbs, tighter curves and more challenging riding. The Old Mine Road, which runs along the Delaware on the New Jersey side of the Water Gap, is one of the oldest roads in the United States, narrow, rough and beautiful. Traffic is moderate, but deer are a constant hazard, and the roads can be busy on weekends.

Hackettstown has fuel stations, diners and cafés, making it a good place to stop. A hearty breakfast at a local diner is a New Jersey tradition. Fill up here before heading into the Water Gap, where services are limited and the scenery takes over.
t.fanwood@40.6,-74.4:
Fanwood is one of those small, tidy New Jersey boroughs built around a railway station, with a compact centre, tree-lined streets and commuters heading for Manhattan each morning. On its own it offers little for a rider beyond a quiet road and a coffee, but its position at the foot of the Watchung Mountains makes it a useful starting point.

The Watchungs are a pair of long, low ridges of basalt, formed by ancient lava flows, that run across northern New Jersey like a natural wall. Their slopes are wooded, and from the top the views stretch east across the plain to the New York skyline. The Watchung Reservation, a large county park on the ridges just north of Fanwood, protects a stretch of forest with a lake, streams and the remains of a deserted village, and the winding roads through it are a pleasant escape from the suburbs. During the Revolution, Washington's army used these ridges as a natural defence, watching the British from the heights.

The riding around Fanwood is mostly suburban, with traffic lights, junctions and moderate traffic. The roads over the ridges are more interesting, with curves and climbs, but they can be busy with local traffic and are patrolled by police. Deer are common in the reservation, and the roads can be slippery with leaves in autumn.

Fanwood and neighbouring Scotch Plains have fuel stations, delis and cafés, and as everywhere in New Jersey, attendants pump the fuel. It makes an easy pause before heading north-west towards the Upper Delaware, where the river winds through forested hills and the road to Hawk's Nest clings to the cliffs above the water.
t.ware@42.3,-72.2:
Ware sits on the Ware River in the middle of Massachusetts, a brick mill town that never quite became a tourist stop and is better company for it. The river powered the factories that built the place, and you can still read that history in the long mill blocks and the tidy grid of streets running down toward the water. For a rider it is the logical doorway to the Quabbin country, the big reservoir that lies a short hop to the west.

Quabbin is the thing to understand about this part of the state. In the 1930s the valley of the Swift River was cleared and flooded to give Boston its drinking water, and four towns, Dana, Enfield, Greenwich and Prescott, went under or were taken apart. t.newport@43.4,-72.2:
Newport is the county seat of Sullivan County, which gives a town of under five thousand people a handsome courthouse and a surprisingly grand common. The Sugar River runs through the middle of it, and the old mill buildings that line the water tell you where the money came from a century and a half ago. Today the town works as a service centre for the surrounding hill country, a place where locals buy their hardware and their pizza and where a rider can do the same.

Newport is also covered-bridge country, with several of the old timber spans tucked into the lanes outside town, and a rail trail follows the river for those who like to walk off a stop. The Richards Free Library on the common is a good-looking stone building that makes a fine backdrop, and the main street keeps the scale of a place that was built before the car arrived.

West toward Claremont the valley opens up, and east toward Sunapee the road climbs into lake country, where glimpses of Lake Sunapee start to appear between the trees. Autumn weekends bring leaf-peepers and slower traffic, so a midweek ride feels like a different place.

As a practical matter, Newport has fuel, groceries and places to sit down, and it is the best-supplied stop for a good distance in either direction. Claremont, about fourteen kilometres away, offers more. Use the town to top off and eat, then take the quiet side roads toward Unity and Sunapee, where traffic thins and the hills do the talking.
t.hull@42.3,-70.9:
Hull is a thin finger of land curling into Massachusetts Bay, and it is one of the most unusual places to start a ride within reach of Boston. The town lies at the end of a long, narrow peninsula, with Nantasket Beach on the ocean side and calm Hingham Bay on the other, so you can see water on both sides of the road for most of the way in. The sense of being at the end of something is real here.

Out on the headland stand the earthworks of Fort Revere, on a hill with a view that takes in the whole harbour, and from the shoreline you can pick out Boston Light, the lighthouse on Little Brewster Island, which has marked the harbour entrance since the eighteenth century. The old Paragon Park amusement park that once crowded the beach has gone, but the carousel survives in the beachfront, a nice link to the days when trolley cars carried families down here for the summer.

Riding in and out follows Nantasket Avenue, Route 228, which runs along the seawall with the Atlantic on your right when heading south. It is flat and straight, not a technical road, but on a clear morning with a little swell breaking on the sand it is easy to forgive it. Wind can be strong, and on hot weekends the beach traffic crawls, so an early start is the answer. Salt and sand work their way onto the asphalt, so be gentle on the first corners.

Hull is a real town of more than ten thousand, so fuel and breakfast are not a worry. Hingham, about seven kilometres away, is the next place of any size and a much calmer harbour town. This is the place to roll the bike to a stop, look out at the horizon, and start the day properly.
t.near queenstown@-45.1,168.5:
South of Queenstown, the road to Kingston follows the eastern shore of Lake Wakatipu, squeezed between deep, cold water and the jagged wall of the Remarkables. In winter they are white to their bases; in summer the bare rock glows gold and grey in the evening light.

Lake Wakatipu is a long, narrow glacial trough shaped like a lightning bolt, and it has a curious habit: its surface rises and falls by several centimetres every few minutes, a slow breathing caused by a standing wave. Māori legend explains it as the heartbeat of the giant Matau, who lies sleeping at the bottom of the lake, his body forming its zigzag shape. The water is clear, startlingly blue and very cold even in summer.

The road south is a good one. It runs along the lake with long sweepers, a few tighter bends and a stretch known as the Devil's Staircase, where it climbs and twists above the water before dropping toward Kingston at the lake's southern tip. Traffic can be heavy with campervans and tourist coaches, many driven by visitors still adjusting to the left side of the road, so give them room. Strong winds can funnel down the lake, and black ice is a real danger on shaded bends in winter.

The rides from here go in two directions. The Milford Road continues south through Kingston and across the plains to Te Anau, then up through the Eglinton Valley and the Homer Tunnel to Milford Sound, one of the world's great mountain roads. The vineyard ride heads the other way, through Frankton and the Kawarau Gorge to Gibbston, Cromwell and Bannockburn, where pinot noir grows on terraces of gravel left by gold miners. The first commercial bungy jump was set up on the Kawarau Bridge, and you can still watch people leap from it.

Fill the tank in Queenstown or Frankton, which have everything. On the way to Milford, Te Anau is the last reliable fuel stop, and there is a long stretch beyond with almost nothing. Bring warm, waterproof layers whatever the season, because weather in Fiordland and around the lakes changes fast.

t.near cromwell@-45.2,169.0:
Cromwell sits where two of Central Otago's big rivers used to meet, and these days the meeting happens under water. When the Clyde Dam was finished in the early 1990s, the rising Lake Dunstan swallowed the old town centre and much of the gorge, and what survived of the gold-era main street was rebuilt as a heritage precinct on the new lakeshore. It is worth the short detour: schist cottages, a bakery or two, and the eerie knowledge that the original riverbank is somewhere below the boats.

The riding around here is a matter of light and space. State Highway 6 runs west through the Kawarau Gorge towards Queenstown, a tight, rocky slot with the milky river far below and bungy jumpers dropping off the old bridge at the far end. North, State Highway 8 heads up past Tarras towards the Lindis Pass, all long tawny hills and wide bends that let you see oncoming traffic a kilometre away. South towards Clyde and Alexandra the road follows the lake through bare schist country that looks almost lunar in the late afternoon.

This is the driest corner of New Zealand, and the summer heat is real; in winter, frost can glaze the shady bends well into the morning, so do not trust the gorge before the sun has been on it. Wind funnels down the lake too, which you will feel on an exposed motorcycle crossing the bridges.

The gold rush of the 1860s first brought people here, but the money now is in stone fruit and wine. Bannockburn, just across the water, grows some of the most southerly Pinot Noir in the world, and roadside stalls sell cherries and apricots in midsummer. Cromwell itself is a proper service town with several fuel stations, supermarkets and cafés, so it is the natural place to fill the tank and eat before the longer, emptier stretches toward Haast, Te Anau or the Lindis, where the next pump can be a long way off.

t.narragansett@41.4,-71.4:
Narragansett is where Rhode Island's south coast stops being a drive and starts being a habit. The town sits on a knuckle of land between Narragansett Bay and the open Atlantic, and the ocean here is the real thing: long gray rollers that arrive from Spain with nothing in between. Ocean Road, Route 1A, hugs the shoreline past the seawall, Scarborough Beach and a string of big shingled summer houses, and on a calm morning it is as pleasant a start to a coast ride as New England offers.

The landmark everybody photographs is the Towers, a pair of stone arches that straddle the road. They are what survived of the Narragansett Pier Casino, a grand resort building designed by McKim, Mead and White in the 1880s that burned in 1900. The arches were left standing, which tells you something about how people here feel about a good ruin. Rhode Island's gilded-age summer crowd once came to this stretch of shore by steamer and train, and the town has been a beach town ever since, with surfers in wetsuits out past the wall even in autumn.

For riding, the point is the pace. Route 1A is slow, with beach traffic, joggers and the occasional stop sign that arrives sooner than you expect, so treat it as a warm-up rather than a speed test. Go early on a summer weekend or choose September, when the water is still warm, the parking lots are half empty and the light has gone golden. South toward Point Judith the land flattens into salt marsh and fishing docks, and the Galilee harbor, where the Block Island ferries leave, is the place for clam cakes and a bowl of chowder. Rhode Island chowder is often clear-brothed, which surprises visitors who expect cream.

Narragansett itself is large enough to have fuel, coffee and everything else you need, and Wakefield-Peacedale a few minutes inland has more supermarkets and stations if you want a choice. Gilbert Stuart, the painter whose portrait of Washington became the image on the dollar bill, was born just up the bay in Saunderstown, and his birthplace is a small museum if you like a detour. The weather is the only real hazard: sea fog can roll in without warning, turning a sunny start into damp visor and cold hands within a few miles.
t.near califon on the way back@40.7,-74.8:
This is the valley of the South Branch of the Raritan River, a trout stream that runs clear enough over its stones to keep fly fishermen loyal for generations. Califon itself is a tiny place, barely a thousand people, with an old railroad right-of-way now used as a rail trail and a main street you will cross before you notice it. Long Valley sits a few kilometres to the north, and the hills on its far side belong to Schooley's Mountain, the first stretch of real ridge you meet when riding in from the east.

The riding here is gentle and rhythmic rather than dramatic. County roads follow the river and then climb over low wooded saddles, with horse paddocks, stone farmhouses and the occasional covered view across the valley. Corners come in long, readable arcs, the surface is mostly decent but patched after hard winters, and speed limits are low and enforced by small-town police who have nothing better to do on a Sunday. Early morning is the best hour, when mist lies in the river bottoms and the few cyclists out are still warming up. Autumn turns the maples loud with colour, and mid-October weekends bring leaf-peepers who slow everything down.

Schooley's Mountain has a more surprising history than its quiet slopes suggest. In the nineteenth century people from New York and Philadelphia came here to take the mineral waters, and big wooden hotels sat along the ridge for the cool air and the cure. The hotels are gone, but the idea that this is a place to escape the city has not changed. Today the ridge is partly preserved as county and state parkland, and the woods hold white-tailed deer in numbers that make dusk riding a genuine hazard. Slow down when the light goes amber.

For practical matters, Califon and Long Valley are both small enough that you should not count on fuel or a late meal in the village itself. Hackettstown, about fourteen kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size and has stations, supermarkets and plenty of places to eat. Beattystown is closer but little more than a crossroads and a few houses. If you are using this point as a start or finish, a swim is possible in the river pools in summer, though the water is cold and the banks are private in places, so ask before you wade in.
t.near woodbury on the way back@41.3,-74.1:
Central Valley is a small community in Orange County, New York, wedged between the Hudson Highlands and the New York State Thruway, and its claim to fame is that it sits beside Woodbury Common, one of the largest outlet shopping centres in the United States. On a weekend the shops draw tour buses from all over the region, and traffic backs up on the approach roads. Woodbury, the larger town about six kilometres away, has about eleven thousand people and plenty of fuel, supermarkets and diners.

Away from the mall, the land rises into the wooded hills of Harriman State Park, a huge protected area that covers more than forty thousand acres of rocky ridges, lakes and old forests. The park was created in the early twentieth century with land donated by the Harriman family, and it is a haven for hikers, with miles of trails crossing the Appalachian Trail. Its main road, the Seven Lakes Drive, winds through the hills with gentle, well-surfaced curves and lakes visible through the trees. It is a delightful ride, though cyclists and families fill it on warm weekends.

The nearby Hudson River, about ten miles east, runs through the Highlands in a deep, narrow valley, and Bear Mountain, with its summit tower, lies close at hand. Route 32 runs north from the area through the hamlet of Highland Mills toward Cornwall and Newburgh, a pleasant road with farms and ponds. Storm King Mountain rises above the river further north, and Route 218, a twisting road on its flank, has some of the most dramatic views on the Hudson.

For riders, the gateway is simple: the exit off the Thruway puts you minutes from the park. Early mornings are quiet, with mist in the valleys, while Saturdays and Sundays bring crowds. Fuel and food are straightforward, and the outlet complex offers coffee and plenty of fast food for those in a hurry. Autumn is the star season, when Harriman glows with colour, and winter closes some park roads. In spring, the redbuds bloom along the hillsides, and the streams run high and loud.
t.near lambertville@40.4,-75.0:
Two towns share the Delaware at Lambertville, and they have been admiring each other across the water for generations. On the New Jersey bank stands Lambertville, all brick Victorian rows climbing the slope from the river; on the Pennsylvania side lies New Hope, linked by an old bridge you can walk or ride across in a minute. Either could be the stop on its own. Together, they make the best place on the Delaware River Scenic Byway for a long, unhurried lunch.

Lambertville has an easy, lived-in feel. Antiques shops fill the old warehouses and storefronts, the flea market on the edge of town is a regular draw, and every spring the town celebrates the shad that run up the river to spawn, a tradition older than most of its buildings. The canal that parallels the river, the Delaware and Raritan, was dug in the nineteenth century to carry coal and goods between the river and the sea, and its towpath is now a quiet footpath under sycamores. Walk a few hundred metres of it if you can, because the water and the trees do a great deal to settle a rider after the traffic.

The river road, Route 29 on the Jersey side, is a pleasant rather than a thrilling ride. It follows the river closely, with the Delaware on one side and low, wooded bluffs on the other, and the corners are gentle bends rather than challenges. Traffic can be heavy on weekend afternoons, especially near the bridge, so go early or midweek if you want the road to yourself. Not far upstream, at Washington Crossing, George Washington's army crossed the ice-choked river on a December night in 1776 before the attack on Trenton, and the park there keeps that story.

Lambertville is a proper town of a few thousand people, so fuel and food are not a worry, though parking on weekends can be a nuisance. Ewing, farther south toward Trenton, is the bigger place for anything unusual. Autumn, when the sycamores along the river go yellow, is the best season; summer is warm and humid, and winter leaves the byway quiet and sometimes icy in the shade.
t.near mendham@40.8,-74.7:
The winter of 1779 to 1780 was one of the harshest on record, and the Continental Army spent it in huts at Jockey Hollow, a few miles east of Mendham, short of food, clothing and pay. Soldiers froze, starved and deserted, and some mutinied, yet the army survived. The site is now part of Morristown National Historical Park, with reconstructed huts, an old farmhouse and quiet woodland trails, and it is a moving place to stop.

Mendham itself is a small, well-kept colonial village in the hills of Morris County, with white churches, old taverns and a crossroads that has been a meeting point for centuries. The surrounding countryside is horse country, with rolling pastures, stone walls, big estates and wooded hills. It is one of the most attractive corners of northern New Jersey, and the roads through it are among the most pleasant in the region.

The riding here is a joy. Roads wind over hills and through valleys, past farms, forests and streams, with constant changes of direction and gradient. The surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel, potholes after winter and horse riders on the lanes. Traffic is moderate, but local drivers can be impatient, and police patrol regularly. In autumn, the leaves turn spectacular colours, and the roads are at their best.

Mendham has a deli, a few cafés and restaurants, and fuel is available nearby, although Morristown, a short ride east, has a wider choice of services. A coffee in the village, followed by a walk at Jockey Hollow, makes a satisfying break. Northwards, the Catskills promise high peaks and longer, wilder roads.
t.near east norwalk@41.1,-73.4:
Nobody will pretend there is a mountain pass in East Norwalk. This is the flat, salty shore of Long Island Sound in south-western Connecticut, where the Norwalk River opens into a harbour full of moorings, boatyards and marsh, with a chain of low rocky islands scattered offshore. East Norwalk is the older, waterside side of the city of Norwalk, with Calf Pasture Beach, a park and a long sandy shore facing the islands.

Norwalk was built on the sea. In the nineteenth century it was one of the great oyster towns of the East Coast, and the beds in the shallow waters around the islands supplied restaurants as far away as Europe; a few oyster boats still work the harbour today. The Norwalk Islands have a lighthouse, on Sheffield Island, reached by a small ferry in summer, and the Maritime Aquarium in South Norwalk tells the story of the Sound and its creatures, from seals to sharks. In the town, the Lockwood-Mathews Mansion, a grand Victorian house built in the 1860s, shows how wealthy the area became.

As a stop on a Catskill and Kaaterskill ride, it is far from the mountains, but it can be a sensible place to begin or end. The Catskills lie a couple of hours to the north, with Kaaterskill Falls, steep cloves and the Hudson River School painters' views, and the route there often goes up the Merritt Parkway, one of the most beautiful roads in the region. The Merritt, opened in the 1930s and 40s, winds through woods with a grassy median and dozens of ornate bridges, each one designed differently, and it is closed to trucks. Motorcycles are allowed, and on a quiet morning it is a joy, though it can be congested at rush hour.

Interstate 95 runs right through Norwalk and is one of the most congested highways in the country, so avoid it if you can. The local roads along the shore and up into the wooded hills of Wilton and New Canaan are much more pleasant, with stone walls, old houses and gentle curves.

East Norwalk has fuel, food and services, and the harbour area has seafood restaurants where you can try local oysters or a lobster roll. Ride down to Calf Pasture Beach, look out at the islands and the boats, and enjoy the salt air before heading north.
t.near deerfield@44.2,-71.7:
It is a lovely, wooded corner of the state, and Littleton, a small mill-turned-tourist town of about four thousand people, lies fifteen kilometres to the northwest, with Whitefield a little farther off. Fuel and food are in those towns.

The riding is a pleasure. The roads here run through forest and river valleys under steep granite mountains, with long, sweeping bends, a few tight curves, and rises and falls that follow the contours of the land. Surfaces are generally good, though frost heaves can be rough in spring, and speed limits are modest. Traffic is moderate on weekdays and heavy on summer and autumn weekends, when visitors come for hiking and foliage. Peak colour comes in late September to mid October, when the maples turn red and orange against the dark spruce, and the roads are at their most beautiful. Moose are a real hazard at dawn and dusk, so slow down in wooded stretches.

The mountains are the story. The White Mountains are the highest range in the northeastern United States, and Mount Washington, at 1,917 metres, is famous for some of the worst weather on Earth, with winds that have been measured at more than 370 kilometres an hour. Franconia Notch, a steep-sided gap nearby, was long the home of the Old Man of the Mountain, a rock profile that collapsed in 2003 and still appears on the state's emblem. The area was a destination for travellers in the nineteenth century, who came by train to grand hotels, painters of the White Mountain school captured its scenery, and the tradition of tourism has continued ever since.

Littleton is worth a stop. It was the birthplace of Eleanor H. Porter, the author of Pollyanna, and a statue of her stands in the town. The main street has a famous candy shop with a very long counter, a few good cafes and old brick buildings along the Ammonoosuc River. The air in the mountains smells of balsam fir, damp earth and woodsmoke, and the streams run cold and clear over granite.

Fill the tank in Littleton, wear a warm layer, since the mountain weather changes quickly, and watch for wildlife.
t.near north adams@42.7,-73.1:
North Adams lies in a bowl of mountains in the far northwest corner of Massachusetts, in the Berkshires, with Mount Greylock, the state's highest peak at about 1,060 metres, rising just to the south. For most of the twentieth century it was a mill town, and the vast brick factory complex on the edge of downtown, once the home of an electrical equipment company, was converted into MASS MoCA, one of the largest contemporary art museums in the country. The town has the slightly worn, determined look of a place that has reinvented itself, and the old brick storefronts have cafes and galleries.

The Mohawk Trail, Route 2, is one of the oldest tourist roads in America, opened in 1914. It follows a path used by Native peoples long before, and it crosses the Hoosac Range with a famous hairpin turn on the western side, where the road drops into North Adams in a tight bend with a view over the valley. Nearby, the Hoosac Tunnel, almost five miles long, was bored through the mountain in the 1850s and 1860s for the railroad, a project that took more than two decades and cost the lives of nearly two hundred workers, and is still in use today. The Western Summit lookout offers a view over the town and toward Vermont and New York.

For the ride, the western climb is the most memorable part. The road climbs steadily out of the valley with a series of tight bends, clear views and good surface, then runs east through forest and farmland along the Cold River. The curves are many and varied, and in the first half of October, when the maples turn red and orange, the road is famously beautiful and crowded. Weekends in foliage season bring heavy traffic, and mid-week is far better. Winter closes parts of the area with snow, and spring can bring mud and frost heaves.

North Adams has several fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and nearby Adams and Williamstown, home to a well-known college, have more. The road east of town has fewer services, with small shops and diners in villages, so fill up in town. A lunch at a diner, with local maple syrup on offer in season, is a pleasant way to rest.

At the hairpin, take care on the outside of the bend, where gravel collects. The view back over the valley is worth a stop.
